speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I turn to another phase? I have perhaps touched at sufficient length on the situation as to there being an emergent condition. Let me come now to the matter of unemployment insurance. Here perhaps I cannot do better than quote first of all what the hon. member for North Winnipeg said when he was speaking on his amendment. In making this quotation, may I say to him and to his neighbour from Winnipeg North Centre and to my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) and to a few others, especially where in order to give point to their remarks they
1230	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
proceed to draw deductions from press reports, that they should in selecting press reports in the first instance be very careful to see that the reports are accurate, and secondly that the quotations are accurate before they put on Hansard quotations or alleged quotations that are not truly representative of what has been said, or in accord with what the press generally has had to say in reporting a matter. I am not saying that my hon. friend did intentionally what I am about to disclose, but I say it served his purpose very well to make a certain quotation in the manner he did. Let me read what, my hon. friend said. On March 31, my hon. friend put the following on Hansard:
In a statement which the right hon. Prime Minister made to this delegation the impression was broadcast that the government was sympathetic and willing to do something to speed forward unemployment insurance. This is what he is reported to have said according to the Ottawa Evening Citizen of February 27:
"Eventually Canada will have a system of unemployment insurance. This was the only constructive way to deal with the unemployment situation and he hoped it would soon be possible to work out an insurance plan. Seasonal measures in the way of relief and public works were of no permanent assistance and an insurance plan offered the only constructive way of avoiding distress. Under it those who employed them would be compelled to contribute to a fund during their periods of employment and the insured would receive benefits when out of work."
That is from the Ottawa Citizen of February 27, 1930.
I have here the Ottawa Citizen of February 27, 1930, with the quotation my hon. friend placed on Hansard, and which he said bore out the point of view that at the time I was committing the government to some scheme of unemployment insurance. This is the quotation:
Eventually Canada will have a system of unemployment insurance.
Please note my non. friend read the quotation as if it went on to say that this was the only constructive way to deal with the unemployment problem. He however left out the important words which follow this first sentence:
Eventually Canada will have a system of unemployment insurance, Premier King predicted yesterday in replying to a deputation seeking federal aid to municipalities and provinces on unemployment relief. This, he said, was the only constructive way to deal with the unemployment situation and he hoped it would soon be jiossible to work out an insurance plan.
In other words, the paragraph I have just read was a lead put in by the newspaper reporter who sent this particular item to the press. It was a lead in which he gave his own

interpretation of the significance of what had been said and which, at most, he characterized as a prediction. May I direct the attention of the house to something further? I do not think this was in any way intentional on the part of my hon. friend, though it is rather singular that he preferred the Citizen version for his quotation. The quotation is:
Under it those who employed them would be compelled to contribute to a fund.
Exactly the same despatch appeared on the same day in the Ottawa Journal and in the Montreal Gazette as well as in other papers, but with an all important additional phrase. Both those papers have the following wording:
Under it those who expected relief and those who employed them would be compelled to contribute to a fund.
My hon. friend used the particular cutting which left out the words:	"Those who expected relief and."

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: What did the Prime Minister say, really?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I explain that I took
the Ottawa Citizen because I thought it would be the paper that would not be unfriendly to the Prime Minister? That is the only reason I quoted from the Ottawa Citizen. I never took the trouble to look at it in any other paper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I accept the
explanation of my hon. friend. May I point out, however, not only to my hon. friend but to any members who are fond of using press references, that before they use them they ought to be perfectly sure that the report is accurate?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: How can they do so?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
By making
comparisons with despatches, in other papers dealing with the same matter; or, as was suggested this afternoon by an hon. member opposite, quoting Hansard instead of the press. My hon. friend by making use of a quotation which omitted all reference to contribution by employees was giving an entirely wrong interpretation of what I said.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: What did the Prime Minister say, really?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I will tell my hon. friend what I said. I have my words here. I will quote from the Montreal Gazette, which my hon. friend would no doubt prefer to any other paper.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have not the slightest
preference, but I would like to know what the Prime Minister did say.

Unemploymen t-
-Mr. Mackenzie King

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Here is what
I said, as reported in the Montreal Gazette of February 27:
Seasonal measures in the way of relief and public works were of no permanent assistance, and an insurance plan offered the only constructive way of avoiding distress. Under it those who expected relief and those who employed them would be compelled to contribute to a fund during their periods of employment and would receive benefits when out of work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Does the Prime Minister
now state that insurance of that character is the only constructive way of giving relief for unemployment in this country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, I do not
say it is the only way, but I say it is one way. I believe many hon. members here present, and I hope my hon. friend will be among them, will live to see the day when a system of social insurance is introduced which will help to relieve labour of many of the fears it now has with respect to unavoidable misfortune. If insurance is a good thing against fire, accident or loss of life, it is at least equally good for the family of the worker against unemployment, one of the many inevitable things he has to face.
May I remind hon. members how it came about that the statement I have referred to was made? It was given on the occasion when the delegation referred to waited on the government. I carefully reviewed, as far as I could, everything material that had been said by those who spoke, I could not state all in the short time at my disposal, but 1 left out so far as I am aware no essential feature. One gentleman-I cannot recall who he was and I do not know whether he was a Liberal, a Conservative, or what he was- in the course of the representations made spoke about unemployment insurance as a means of dealing with the problem. Stating my own views on the question, I said that I agreed with the gentleman who had said that unemployment insurance was one constructive way of dealing with the problem of unemployment. That is how the remark came about. Nothing further was said in regard to it. Out of that, however, whoever wrote the despatch wrote the interesting lead to the effect that there was a prediction that unemployment insurance would some day come about. I think that is a perfectly sound prediction, but it is a very different thing from saying that I was committing the government and parliament to a system of social or unemployment insurance. I merely stated a position as I believe it to be correct.
In order to make my attitude clear, I ought perhaps to say that my views on labour problems are not born of to-day. They are not put forward at this time or at this moment for the purpose of seeking political or party gain. I have strong convictions on some of these questions that affect the well being of the masses of the people, and I have expressed them in a manner which anybody who wishes to be acquainted with them can soon discover.
It has been said:
Oh that mine adversary had written a book.
I have in my hands a book written by myself over some thirteen years ago. At that time I was not in parliament, nor was I then thinking of reentering parliament. I was, however, thinking about the problems that other countries and we in this country would have to face in the days of reconstruction after the great war. I sought to turn to advantage, along with my studies, such experience as I had had in public life, and wrote this book which is entitled Industry and Humanity-A Study in the Principles Underlying Industrial Reconstruction. In stating those principles I set out clearly what I felt and believed in regard to labour problems and the only or most effective means of their solution. Amongst other subjects I naturally touched upon the problem of employment. At page 237 of this volume I find the following:
It is the fear of unemployment which lies at the root of most of the minor fears which labour entertains. The fear of unemployment is in reality the fear on the part of labour that capital will not be provided to carry on industry continuously, and under conditions which will afford adequate remuneration to effort. It is an outgrowth of the fallacy that quantity of work is necessarily limited. This fear gives rise to the fear that the introduction of new machinery, or the increased use of machinery already installed, will displace labour; the fear that speeding-up processes will diminish work; the fear that female, child, unskilled, or imported labour will be substituted for skilled; the fear that men of one trade will encroach upon the work for which men of other trades have been specially trained: the fear that the number of apprentices will be so increased as to lessen the requirement for skilled hands; and the fear that long hours and continuous overtime will exhaust employment.
That is but one reference to unemployment. I did not, however, stop at a mere mention of the case, but I wrote what I believed to be one of the remedies for the situation. On page 345 is the following reference to social insurance, of which unemployment insurance is one form:
Social insurance, which in reality is health insurance in one form or another, is a means employed in most industrial countries to bring
1232	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
about a wider measure of social justice, without, on the one hand, disturbing the institution of private property and its advantages to the community, or, on the other, imperilling the thrift and industry of individuals. Social insurance looks upon industry as in the nature of social service.
Here may I say a word to my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland)? He said yesterday that industry should not be a mere device for making profits. I agree with him absolutely. I believe we will get no solution of the problems of industry until we get the conception, yes until the world gets the conception that industry is not a mere device for the making of profits but that industry is in the nature of social service, and that every one who contributes to industry, whether it be by his capital, labour, or skill as a manager, is playing a part in the nature of a social service. Until we get that idea into the minds of the people and have our legislation based upon it, we will not reach a solution of unemployment or of any other social problem.
I quote further:
Social insurance looks upon industry as in the nature of social service. It regards the owner of land or capital as a capitalist, but ailso as a public trustee. It looks upon the worker in industry as a wage-earner, but equally as a necessary member of the community. It places the emphasis on personality rather than on property, and on life rather than on wealth.
Insurance against unemployment recognizes that an isolated human being, not less than a machine, must be oared for when idle. It recognizes also that nothing is so dangerous to the standard of life, or so destructive of minimum conditions of healthy existence, as widespread or continued unemployment. Where idleness is the fault of the social order, rather than of the individual concerned, it places the onus on the state to safeguard its own assets, not more in the interest of the individual than in the interest of social well-being.
Workmen's compensation, sickness and invalidity insurance, widows' pensions, maternity and infant benefits, recognize wherein personal relationships in industry have changed, and where as a consequence of new conditions permanent handicaps arise. The social legislation of which these measures are an expression rejects, as unworthy, the thought that men and wmen voluntarily incur accident, sickness, disease, enfeebled health, or dependence in distress, any more than they willingly seek enslavement of any kind. It recognizes the difficulty of differentiating between industrial accident and occupational disease; and between disease occasioned by occupation or its environments and illness otherwise contracted; also the impossibility of dissociating from economic conditions the social waste caused by excessive and preventable illness. It sees that debt binds health as it binds freedom, that sickness represents the most frequent factor of individual destitution, and that it is in painful crisis that handicaps for the whole of life are ofitenest imposed. To save the spirit of men from being crushed is quite as important 
as to prevent their bodies from being broken or infected. Many a niatn's spirit tails when, through no fault of his own, or of his family, efficiency is permanently impaired through accident, or savings become exhausted by unemployment or sickness, or where a new life in the home suggests an additional burden instead of a joy. Much invalidity and penury is due to lack of character and thrift; but much also is evidence of want of effective social control. What society fails effectively to prevent, society is in some measure under obligation to mend.
There is the statement I made at that time with respect to social insurance. I then proceed to give my views with respect to old age pensions, and by the view as expressed in this volume I stand now and am prepared to stand for the remainder of my life.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What does the Prime
Minister mean by the word "state"?
Mr. MACKENZIE KING; I will come to that. May I point out that at page 348, I had this to say:
It is the elimination of fears with respect to these fundamental requisites of health that labour speaks of as a national minimum standard of life.
I then point out wherein the Labour party of Great Britain put forward as its first principle the universal enforcement of the national minimum, and if my hon. friends care to go a little further they will find another statement at page 353. I might draw attention to the fact that this statement was in print sometime before the terms of the labour convention of the treaty of Versailles, was drafted:	'
It is not a national minimum only, but an international minimum, which is needed, if labour standards are to be protected against the undermining effects of the law of competing standards operating through international competition. The possible creation of some international agency to further the establishment and enforcement of international conventions aimed at the maintenance of an international minimum, is a subject of momentous concern.
It is well deserving of consideration in any discussion pertaining to a League of Nations which may constitute a part of the peace negotiations at the conclusion of the war.
There is a statement of my belief that the industrial problem, whether it relates to unemployment, accident, o^ age, disease, invalidity or otherwise, never will be solved satisfactorily to any nation or to any country until we have an international minimum standard of health which will prevail in all the countries of the world.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friend laughs. He may well laugh; I am not surprised, because he has not always had-well.

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
I will not say what I had in mind. My hon. friend will find out one of these days, if he comes to interest himself in industrial problems, that in seeking a final solution he will have to take notice of what is happening in every part of the world, and will have to take account of the industrial standards that exist in all parts of the world. There is a law familiarly known as Gresham's law, which asserts that where two metals are in circulation, the one pure and the other base, if the metals are left in circulation long enough the base will drive out the pure. That law has been demonstrated to be true with regard to the precious metals in circulation in every country. The same law is I believe discoverable with respect to competing standards of health, or other standards of living and working conditions. Bring into competition a lower standard with a higher standard, and sooner or later the lower standard will drive the higher standard out of existence altogether. That is why the League of Nations, representing all the countries of the world, is seeking to bring about among the different nations uniform standards with respect to matters of health and working conditions and those matters dealt with by social legislation generally.
As far as the British Empire is concerned, as I said a moment ago, I believe its standards in industry and health are higher, taking it by and large, than those of any other political entity on earth. I believe also that within the British Empire we in Canada have higher standards for labour generally, and better working conditions, than exist in any other part of the empire, which means that our standards are the best in the world. If however, we are to maintain our standards it can be done only by the raising to our level of the standards of other countries that enter into competition with us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Or by protecting our workmen from that competition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, I expected to hear that from my hon. friend! Shut ourselves in and do nothing for anyone else. Last night my hon. friend was speaking on the birth of Christianity. I believe I can show him that no man lives unto himself alone, and that it is only by helping his neighbour that eventually he will help himself, and that the same is true of a nation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: But in the meantime will the Prime Minister allow the unemployed in Canada to be subjected to the competition of those working under the lower standard to which he himself has referred, until such standard is raised to our level?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am not dealing with a momentary situation; I am dealing with this industrial question in a broad way and as a world problem. I am not dealing with what is going to happen inside a circle around which a ring fence can be put.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I would remind the Prime Minister that he cannot put a ring fence around Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I stand by
what I have said, that our own standards can be ultimately maintained only as the standards are raised to a like level in all competing countries. There are apparently some who hold to the idea of building up around Canada a tariff wall which will shut her off from competition with any and every other country in the world. For the next month or two we shall hear about the erection of tariff walls which will serve to restrict our trading with the countries of the world. But were this to occur, what would be the position shortly after such a policy had been effected? More and more in the way of unemployment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is high enough now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
When we fail to keep it
high enough it brings about unemployment in this country, but creates employment in other countries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. member for East Calgary asked me about the resolutions of the convention with respect to labour in the peace treaty of Versailles, and I think he as well as some other hon. members in the course of their remarks commented upon the fact that the Liberal party had incorporated into its platform the various principles which were laid down in the labour convention of the treaty of Versailles. That is perfectly correct; and let me say that the liberal party of Canada was the first political party in the world to incorporate in its platform those principles; and they were incorporated in their entirety. I think I am safe in saying that those principles have not been more fully recognized or maintained by any other country in the world than they have been by Canada. I would like to quote them to the house.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Were they not framed
by Sir Robert Borden?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not think Sir Robert Borden ever saw them until they were printed, though he may have. At the Liberal convention in August, 1919, I presented a resolution which reads as follows-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Is this the chart?
1234	COMMONS
Unemploymen t-Mr. Mackenzie King

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If the hon.
member will look at the chart he will be amazed at how far we have gone in the directions indicated. I said:
I have the privilege of presenting to this gathering a resolution of the committee on the subject of labour and industrial relations. I shall read the resolution first, and then address myself to the subjects and contents mentioned in it:
"Resolved that the committee recommends that the National Liberal Convention accepts in their entirety as a part of the Liberal platform, in the spirit in which they have been framed and in so far as the special circumstances of the country will permit, the terms of the labour convention and general principles associated with the League of Nations and incorporated in the conditions of peace.
"These methods and principles for regulating labour conditions set forth in the treaty are as follows: "
I ask you to note these words, "as set forth in the treaty,"
The question was raised by some hon. member as to whether or not I had used the phrase that labour was merely a commodity, and I think that question will be answered by the following:
I ask you to note these words, "as set forth in the treaty," because the committee thought it well to make an exact copy of what is contained in the treaty itself.
"First-The guiding principle that labour should not be regarded merely as a commodity or article of commerce."
With regard to that, I said:
Had the committee been framing that resolution themselves, I think that they would have omitted the word "merely." The labourer and his labour cannot be separated, and the members of the committee feel that the resolution would be stronger and would more fully express the sentiments which they have at heart if it read:
"First-The guiding principle that labour should not be regarded as a commodity or article of commerce."
The word "merely" being left out. But we prefer to take the exact wording of the articles as drawn up at the peace conference.
"Second-The right of association for all lawful purposes by the employed as well as by the employers."
I think that principle has been generally recognized in Canada. The next clause reads:
"Third-The payment to the employed of a wage adequate to maintain a reasonable standard of life as this is understood in their time and country."
This administration has stood four-square for the principle as there enunciated. That it was a principle of the Liberal party was demonstrated in the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, whose government was the first in Canada to introduce a fair wages resolution and to put it in force in government contracts.

Liberal administration was the first to create in this country a department of labour in the federal government. The Liberal administration was the first to put upon the statute books of Canada laws respecting conciliation and arbitration in industrial disputes. I could mention many other such reforms initiated by Liberal administrations. The next clause reads:
"Fourth-The adoption of an 8-hour day or a 48-hours week as the standard to be aimed at where it has not already been obtained."
May I remind the house that there is now before parliament a bill w'hich has been introduced by the present administration through the Minister of Labour to make the eight-hour day compulsory to the extent that the parliament of Canada can do so with respect to the employees of the federal public service and persons employed under contracts for Dominion public works. The next clause reads:
"Fifth-The adoption of a weekly rest of at least twenty-four hours w-hich should include Sunday wherever practicable."
I think that for the most part has been accomplished. There may be cases where it was not observed; where they exist I think they should be at once eliminated. No man should in carrying out the duties of his occupation be required to work or to absent himself from his family for seven days in the week; nor should any woman have to do so. Labour on six days in the week should be enough, no matter what the occupation. The next clause reads:
"Sixth-The abolition of child labour and the imposition of such limitations on the labour of young persons as shall permit the continuation of their education and assure their proper physical development."
The problem of child labour comes under provincial jurisdiction; we have nothing to do with it beyond obeying in our own field the principle laid down. So far as the present administration is in a position so to do it will continue to lend its influence in support of this principle.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE

and the like, is to my mind conclusive evidence that the provinces were intended to be the ones primarily concerned with all such phases of the industrial situation. Clause 7 reads:

So far as we have to do with that matter, we have recognized it. The next clause reads:
Ninth-"Every state should make provision for a system of inspection in which women should take part, in order to insure the enforcement of the laws and regulations for the protection of the employed."

speechtext:
What is meant by the

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I intended to
anticipate my hon. friend's question, but he was too quick. It means the recognized political entity possessing the necessary authority. In the case of Canada under our constitution as drafted the state would mean not the federal government, but the governments of the several provinces. The clause reads:
Ninth-"Each state should make provision for a system of inspection in which women should take part in order to insure the enforcement of the laws and regulations for the protection of the employed."
The laws and regulations for the protection of the employed come within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces; they would be the state so far as enactment and enforcement are concerned. We could not appoint women inspectors to enforce these laws even if we wished; we have no authority. The day may come when it will be thought desirable, and I believe that in the course of years industrial legislation in all the provinces will be made uniform. I hope the day will come when legislation regarding industrial matters will be uniform in all the countries of the world, because until that day does come the attainment of higher standards will continue to be prejudiced by possible invasion and undermining by the lower standards.
Those were the principles incorporated in the convention of the League of Nations and they were adopted by the Liberal party in its platform. Every one of those principles has been lived up to and fulfilled as far as has
been possible. But we went still further in dealing with labour problems. Our resolution reads:
And further resolved:
1.	That the introduction into the government of industry of principles of representation whereby labour and the community, as well as capital, may be represented in industrial control, and their interests safeguarded and promoted in the shaping of industrial policies.
We have sought, wherever we could, to see that labour's voice should be heard with respect to matters of industrial policy with which labour was concerned.
2.	-

That in so far as may be practicable-
"Practicable" means amongst other things having regard to what is set out in the constitution of the country.
-having regard for Canada's financial position, an adequate system of insurance against unemployment, sickness, dependence in old age. and other disability, which would include old age pensions, widows' pensions, and maternity benefits, should be instituted by the federal government in conjunction with the governments of the several provinces; and that on matters pertaining to industrial and social legislation an effort should be made to overcome any question of jurisdiction between the Dominion and the provinces by effective cooperation between the several governments.

I have already explained pretty fully the reasons why I take the position I do in seeking to defend the federal treasury and in so doing to keep to their respective fields of effort both the provinces and the Dominion. When on a previous occasion we were discussing this matter of grants from one treasury to another, I said I thought it was an unsound principle; in fact, I think I used the expression that it was a vicious principle to have one body raise the taxes and another body spend the people's moneys thus raised. Is there any hon. member who will disagree with me in that statement? There is none. That is the extent of the statement I made. I was referring to a principle of financing, speaking simply in relation to what is sound and what is unsound in financing. Anyone interested in financing, whether of a municipality, a province, a dominion, an empire, or a league of nations, will, I think, admit it is unwise, an unsound, a wrong principle for one body to have to do with raising the taxes and another to be concerned with the spending of the money so raised, that other body not having to account to the representatives of those who have paid the taxes.

May I point
this out to my hon. friend: When the Dominion was formed certain obligations were placed on the provinces and certain on the Dominion. It was recognized at that time that in connection with the confederation agreement it was necessary, and might continue to be necessary, to give to the provinces certain specific amounts in order to make the balances even, if I may so express it. In other words, what the fathers of confederation were seeking to do was to give each a distinctive field or jurisdiction; but they recognized that in giving to each a distinctive field the provinces would to a certain degree be handicapped in the matter of raising revenues, and they met that situation by fixing certain definite subsidies to be paid from the federal treasury to the provinces. Those subsidies had no strings of any kind attached to them. They became the complete property of the provinces to deal with as they pleased, and were so recognized as part of the pact of confederation. That in itself is, I submit, a reason why we should not go further in dealing with federal moneys in relation to the provinces. If the provinces have not enough money to carry on their functions as assigned to them by the constitution of this country, then there should be a further revision of the financial terms of confederation. There has been already, may I say, one or two financial revisions for that purpose. We should give to the provinces what, if any, is their due, in that regard. But once we have given them subsidies of a specific amount and said that they are free to deal with them as they see fit, they should not be permitted to come to the federal treasury for additional amounts, one day for highways, another for technical education, another for old age pensions-one thing after another, apparently without limit. I am speaking now wholly from the point of view of what I regard as sound financing.
To make my position perfectly clear, may I say this? I have been from the beginning one of the strongest advocates of technical education. I believe in transcontinental highways and in other highways. I believe in old age pensions. I believe in unemployment insurance. I believe in all these things, but if they are to be carried out it must be done in accordance with the spirit as well as the letter of the constitution. Discussing this matter on the 21st of February of last year, I said:
May I direct -attention to this further fact which bears immediately upon the grants from the federal treasury to the provinces.

When he looks at that text he will find that I began and ended with a reference to the principle of financing, and that what I said had nothing whatever to do with the question of whether the principle of old age pensions was sound or unsound. I believe that everyone who has given any attention to public finance will agree that it is a thoroughly vicious system to have one body raise taxes and another body expend the money thus secured. In other words, give to the prov-

inces these grants from the federal treasury, without their being obliged to raise the money themselves by taxation, and you will not get, with respect to expenditure, that careful supervision which would be exercised if the provinces themselves were obliged to raise the money in the first instance. It is a bad system, a thoroughly vicious system, and that is the reason why the present administration has been seeking to put an end to a system that grew up at a time when the country was in the throes of war or had to meet a post-war situation-a system which, had it been permitted to develop, would have become thoroughly destructive of anything in the shape of economy with respect to the expenditure of the people's money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I had hoped to have opportunity to devote some part of my remarks to enlarging a little on the constructive side of this question of unemployment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friends need not laugh. I will give them twenty minutes of it. May I say of the addresses that have been delivered in the course of this debate, I think the most thoughtful and the most helpful, if I may distinguish between them, was the one made by my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland). He did seek to give to the house some appreciation of at least one very important phase of the problem of unemployment. He did so, I thought, exceptionally well, and in a manner which revealed full and careful study. His remarks

had largely to do with the effect of discoveries and inventions, and he pointed out how through the course of the years under the agency of invention and of discovery labour was repeatedly being placed in the position where it was finding its former occupations disappearing and was forced to get new training or to go into some new branch of trade or industry or was left by the wayside altogether. My hon. friend went on to suggest that it would be well for the government to appoint a commission to make a survey of conditions in the country bearing on the question of unemployment. May I say this to him? If I believed a survey would throw any light whatever on the problem beyond what we already possess, I would recommend to my colleagues the appointment of a commission for the purpose. But my hon. friend's own speech was the best answer that could be made as to where a commission would be wholly inadequate to deal at all effectively with this situation. The situation that faces labour, as we look ahead a few years, is going to arise out of conditions that are largely unforeseen at the present moment. New inventions are coming, new discoveries are going to be made which will bring other processes into existence and eliminate in part, if not altogether, certain of the callings and trades and employment connected therewith, that are being carried on at the present time, and these changes will inevitably bring about unemployment to large numbers of men. Discoveries of new processes brought about by scientific research, discoveries of new portions of the earth's surface and of much that lies beneath the surface, and methods of production, distribution and exchange-these things are going to recur and recur throughout the future, and no commission appointed will ever be able to anticipate what may come about in that regard. More than that, unless I have failed altogether to convey to hon. members the conception I have of this labour problem, namely, that it is a world problem, it must be apparent that conditions so far as this country is concerned in matters of unemployment are going to depend, not so much on what is going to happen in Canada itself in the first instance as on what happens outside and beyond the bounds of this country. No commission can foresee what will happen. Let me take the opening parts of my hon. friend's speech. He very straightforwardly said that the present depression so far as it exists was due, first of all, to the western wheat crop not being as large as it had been in previous years; in the second place, to the fact that the crop had not been marketed to anything like the extent

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
it had been in former years; and in the third place, to the railway earnings and other earnings being smaller in consequence. He spoke about conditions in Great Britain and the extent to which the markets over yonder were being affected by what had taken place and was taking place in other countries. He also referred to the collapse which took place on the stock exchange. My hon. friend is right in stating that these are in the main the causes that account for any existing depression and consequent unemployment; but what body of experts could have foreseen so long as a year ago that anything erf the kind was about to happen?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was not so much my purpose that the commission should examine into the actual causes of unemployment as to try to find a solution for it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am pointing out to my hon. friend that the solution cannot be found in any one formula; it cannot be found in any one method. It can only be found by each authority doing what it can within its own jurisdiction, and in cooperation with all other authorities. It is moreover a world problem.
My hon. friend asks for a solution of this question. I tell him that the only way in which this country can hope to solve the unemployment problem to the degree to which it is possible for it alone to solve it, is not by the adoption of some single measure relating specifically to unemployment, but by making prevail in regard to all its policies those principles which will make for greater productivity in our country and for an increase in employment as a consequence. May I point out that at the end of the term of office of every Conservative administration which has been in power in Canada and has sought to enforce its doctrines of high protection, we have had a period of depression such as had not before existed in the country's history. May I point out with some degree of pride that whenever Canada has a Liberal administration holding office for any length of time, after the first few years the country has begun to show prosperity. Prosperity has rapidly increased. This has not been due to chance; it has been due to a difference in the policies which have been put into force by Conservative and Liberal governments respectively. When the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into office in 1896 it found this country in a condition of depression, the like of which had not been known theretofore in the history of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman
remember 1877 or 1878?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am not as old as my hon. friend, but I do remember 1896. I remember the discussions of the industrial situation as it existed at the time. From the day Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power conditions began to improve and from then until the day he left office this country enjoyed more in the way of prosperity than at any previous time. It was a golden era. I will come down to more recent times; I will come to the time of the present administration. What are the facts? When we came into office in 1921 what did we find? We found that the public debt was being increased at the rate of $92,000,000 per year; we found a condition of extreme depression. We heard for some time after nothing but cries of blue ruin and whispers of death. Our railroads were disorganized, and throughout the country everything was in about as bad a condition as it could possibly be. What has been the change? Once our policies were given a chance to take effect, from that time on we have witnessed steady reduction in the debt of the country, steady reduction in taxation, increase in production, increase in trade, increase in industry in its several branches, and a degree of prosperity which has not been paralleled since the days of Laurier, and which has never been equalled in the history of our country. I say to my hon. friend from Bow River, and I hope he will agree with me, that during the next few years more will depend upon the policies of the government with respect to trade and production than upon anything else-upon wise fiscal policies. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition talks about sending raw materials out of the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I say to the right hon. gentleman that more depends on trade and consumption in the next few years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friend
the leader of the opposition suggests as a remedy that we must not allow the export of any of our raw materials or their manufacture in other countries. I notice my hon. friends have published within the past day or two a small political pamphlet in which amongst other things that argument is stressed. What are the raw materials of this country which my hon. friend is going to stop being sent out if and when he assumes office? Will his policy apply to agricultural products? Will he prevent raw materials of that kind going out?

1242	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, the United States is doing that now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What would
Canada not give at this time if we could only market more of our raw materials in the way of grains and other agricultural products? What would Great Britain not give at this time if she could find wider markets for her coal, which is another raw material? Every country is blessed by Providence with certain great resources. They are at different stages of development; it does with these resources as is best for the country itself. In regard to mining, we have vast resources from which there are raw materials we must export if we are to gain the advantage we should from their possession. We cannot consume in any form a fraction of these raw materials within the country itself. In connection with one or two classes of minerals we may possess more than other parts of the world, something of a monopoly, but generally throughout the world these things are distributed amongst the different countries. If we do not continue to sell them some other country will, and we shall lose the market we already have. Is my hon. friend going to stop the export of the products of the different mines that exist in different parts of Canada to-day? I wonder where the working men who are employed in mining operations will get their wages when that sort of thing begins. Where will the home markets be when we lose the markets we have across the seas or to the South and which through our exports we have worked so hard to gain? When it comes to fisheries, another great natural resource, will we stop their export too? And what about our lumber, the products of the forest, is that trade too to be stopped? If we are going to prohibit the export of our raw material will other nations continue to send their raw materials to us.
To-day my hon. friends opposite were talking about our trade with the United States. They know very well that we receive more in a year in the way of raw materials from the United) States than we send to the United-States. If we are going to refuse to send raw materials to other countries, can we expect them to contract to trade in raw materials with us? What about our iron and steel industry? We get most of the raw material, most of the iron ore, from the United States, and the whole iron and steel industry in our country is largely dependent upon it. Are my hon. friends going to say: We will give nothing in the shape of raw materials to a country that supplies us with these essentials to our own industry? What about our cotton industry? We get most of our raw cotton

from the United States. It gives work to thousands of men here. Is my hon. friend's policy one which will stop the trading back and forth in these raw materials in which each of us has a special advantage?
Hon. gentlemen opposite are fond of talking about the home market; it is not the home market they are thinking about so much as a monopoly of the home market for the benefit of a feiw of their privileged friends. Does my hon. friend know we will be able to have a home market -in this country only as we have purchasing power, and that we will get purchasing power only as we are able to sell our products in the markets of the world? The wider your foreign trade, the better will be your home trade. I tell my hon. friend that by his policy and the policy of his friends no ships will be going out of Vancouver or Halifax harbours. When we get what my hon. friend spoke about a moment ago, a tariff wall around this country which will keep everything fro-m coming in and as a consequence prevent everything from going out, you will soon have again the condition of stagnation and unemployment which we have witnessed in previous times.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I rise to a question ol
privilege.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I should like to finish my remarks.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This is a question of
privilege, Mr. Speaker. A few minutes ago I dealt with the "vicious principle" of old age pensions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I submit that my hon. friend wishes to deprive me of the next five minutes in which I should like to finish my speech.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is not so, I have just received this from the library.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A few minutes ago I stated my recollection of a statement which was made last year by the right hon. Prime Minister. I stated he had said that the payment of money to the provinces by the Dominion for old age pensions was a thoroughly vicious principle. I now read from page 316 of Hansard of last year:
Mr. Ladner: What about old age pensions?
Mr. Mackenzie King:	I am glad my hon.
friend speaks of that. There is another case where we are giving to the provinces a lot of money in addition to what they are raising.
Mr. Ladner:	Is that vicious?

Unemployment-Mr. Guthrie
Mr. Bennett:	A thoroughly vicious principle.
Mr. Mackenzie King:	I think it is, yes. I
have come to the conclusion that it is a thoroughly vicious principle.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That has been read before; I read it myself.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: You denied the statement, and so did the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning).

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend the mover of this resolution that when he introduced his amendment he was no doubt anxious to provide an opportunity to discuss the general question of unemployment. It is unfortunate that my hon. friend found it necessary to introduce the matter in the form of an amendment on going into supply. Probably he did so because he felt it to be his only opportunity, and that if he did not do so someone else might get ahead of him.
May I say to my hon. friend: that I hope when the debate is concluded he will feel that his purpose has been served and that we will have had a sufficient discussion of this question? I think the debate will run on in all likelihood for another day or two, and by the time it is finished I hope he will feel that the discussion has been ample, and that he will ask to have his amendment withdrawn. I do not think my hon. friend wishes to be put in the position of opposing the policies with regard to labour and other matters for which this government stands, and I do not think he wishes to place this government in the position where supply cannot be granted. We cannot accept his amendment for the reason that amongst other things we would be voting against the granting of our own supply. If permission to withdraw his amendment is not given by the unanimous consent of the house he and others might I think very well take the view that the discussion has accomplished the purpose he had in view.
May I say to my hon. friends who sit diagonally opposite that before very long they will find out-and particularly those who come from the western provinces-that hon. gentlemen opposite are anxious to unite in a vote with them in an effort to further their policies of higher protection. Hon. members opposite want to have those who are members of the Labour party and those who are members of the Progressive party vote with them on an amendment on going into supply. They desire that so that when we come to our next budget debate-because this has been practically a budget debate-they can claim this division as evidence that there is an unemployment problem due in some way to the policies of
2419-79)
the present government, and that the policies that should be adopted are not those of this government or policies that may be akin, but, the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite, which we know are now and always will be simply matters of increased protection. I ask hon. members to study the position into which they are being drawn in connection with this particular debate. So far as the wording of the amendment is concerned we cannot accept it for still another reason. By implication it suggests that the government is not seeking to do anything in the matter of the relief of unemployment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is true-or
at least I put the question: is it not true?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I just
say this: my belief is that every major policy of the government has some bearing on the question of unemployment. I believe the policies of the present administration have brought our country from depression to prosperity and helped as nothing else could have done to lessen unemployment. I believe my hon. friend who has just interrupted is sincere in his desire to help labour and his fellow men. I wish he would believe that there are other hon. members in this house who are just as anxious as he is to do the same. Just because we do not see eye to eye with him on his particular nostrum, I hope he will not believe that we have not as much heart and soul as those who may label themselves the friends of labour to the exclusion of all others.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this discussion, but a day or two ago I received from the riding which,I have the honour to represent in this house, communications which stated that on account of the unemployment in the city in which I live, it was considered to be my duty to lay before the government and before the house the real situation existing not only in that city but throughout the western portion of Ontario.
Since the opening of parliament I have been under the impression that there was but one opinion in this house as to the existence of a very critical situation with regard to employment or unemployment; I thought that it had been a matter of common knowledge

Unemployment-Mr. Guthrie
for months past in every quarter of the house and in every quarter of the country that such conditions existed. This matter has been referred to continually in the newspapers of the country regardless of their political affiliations; hardly a day passes that public attention is not drawn to this vital question. I have come to the conclusion after hearing members discussing this matter in the corridors of this house that there is but one mind on the subject, that unemployment does exist in Canada to a very grave extent. Until I heard the speech delivered this afternoon by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) I was not aware that there were two opinions in the matter. I have listened with the greatest interest to the remarks of the hon. members for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) and East Calgary (Mr. Adshead), as well as to the speeches delivered by hon. members on the other side of the house, notably by the hon. members for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson) and North Battle-ford (Mr. McIntosh), and by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan). Not one of those hon. members attempted to deny that a serious condition exists in the matter of unemployment; until the Prime Minister spoke this afternoon it was accepted as the real situation.
I am inclined to think that the Prime Minister is significantly misinformed in regard' to the conditions with respect to unemployment. I can well understand that the cry of the unemployed has not penetrated the comfortable seclusion of the Prime Minister of Canada, but I cannot understand why the Minister of Labour was not aware to the fullest extent of all the facts. We who are not connected with the government know a great deal about this question. We cannot shut our eyes to the facts; we know that they exist; we know that deputations have come to Ottawa to meet the Minister of Labour and have laid before him the true facts. The minister in the course of his three-hour speech did not attempt to deny those statements of fact, but he offered absolutely no suggestions for relief. As for the right hon. Prime Minister he boldly proclaimed that the government intended -to do nothing.
The resolution before the house is very plain; it is merely that immediate action be taken to deal with the question of unemployment. The Prime Minister has told us to-day that there is practically no unemployment in this country. Have my hon. friends of the labour movement misrepresented this situation? Are they uninformed as to the true situation? Is the Minister of Labour uninformed? He did not deny the actual fact,

but he could not give us any figures. Is the right hon. the Prime Minister correct in his attitude? What does he see in this plain, simple, direct amendment which evidently causes him so much alarm? As soon as I first read the amendment I thought that it was one which would be accepted unanimously by this house. In my own innocent way I thought that the Prime Minister would so manage matters as to be able to announce to the house that he would accept this amendment, not as a motion of want of confidence but as something which carried with it the unanimous approval of parliament. He did not take that course, but he suggests that in some way or other my hon. friends who represent labour in general are to be inveigled into adopting an attitude which they do not desire to adopt, they are to associate themselves with the Conservative opposition, which association will lead inevitably to disaster. That is something -the Prime Minister has conjured up in his own mind. He asks that the amendment be withdrawn, which amendment would have been unanimously approved by this house were it not for the speech of the Prime Minister. I hope sincerely that the words of my right hon. friend had no influence upon the hon. member for North Winnipeg. The hon. member has moved a resolution which will be strongly supported in parliament, a step in the right direction, taken at the proper time. All he asks is that action be taken to remedy a grievance, and one of national extent. Should we not seek some remedy now, or should we be bluffed out of it by the high sounding phrases of the Prime Minister, who says in effect that he will not believe in a condition of unemployment unless the premiers of the various provinces bring the matter to his attention? Does he not feel that the members of parliament represent all the provinces of confederation? For all federal purposes we are -the representatives of the provinces, and we bring to the attention of parliament the fact that in the various provinces there is an extreme, an emergent condition, and that it is -the duty of parliament to take action under this emergency.
I have watched the career of the Prime Minister since he came into parliament. I am sorry he is not present to-night. I remember well when he entered parliament in 1908; and I refer to this matter because from his speech to-day and one on another occasion, one would imagine that he had been the great champion of the rights of labour since he entered the Canadian House of Commons. I heard him proclaim to-day what he had done in regard to technical education. What

Unemployment-Mr. Guthrie
are the facts? I know they are within Your Honour's knowledge. At the request of various organized labour bodies throughout Canada, in the year 1909 I had the honour of introducing into the House of Commons, while my right hon. friend was Minister of Labour in this parliament, a resolution asking for the appointment of a committee to investigate the question of technical education in order that the Dominion parliament might take some action in the matter. I was supported by two or three on the Liberal side of the house, where I then sat. What was the attitude of the then Minister of Labour, the present Prime Minister of this country? He rose in his place and after a long speech, he killed my motion; he moved the adjournment of the debate to put my motion to the foot of the list. I would not stand for his motion. We divided the house, and on that occasion for the first time I had the honour of voting with the Conservative party. But my right hon. friend called upon his followers who were in the majority to vote down the motion on technical education, and it was voted down. Much time did not elapse after the end of that session before the attitude of my right hon. friend entirely changed. He got busy. The labour unions communicated with him, and very soon thereafter by order in council he appointed the commission which he would not let parliament vote to appoint. Before that commission made a report to the House of Commons my right hon. friend was out of the house. He was out of the house from 1911 to 1919 and he had no more to do with the question of technical education. All he did was to kill the first motion. The Conservative party was in power when the grant was made by parliament to the various provinces in respect of technical education. He was not present either to support or to oppose the grant, but later on when he was in power as Prime Minister, he put an end to that grant and the provinces now do not enjoy a dollar from the Dominion treasury for technical education.
My right hon. friend said this afternoon that if a time ever comes when there is cooperation in this country between the federal authority and the provincial authorities in regard to labour, it will be a happy day for Canada. Does any hon. member think my right hon. friend this afternoon advanced the cause of cooperation by the statements which he made on two occasions when in this house he proclaimed a new policy, a new doctrine; when he announced on two occasions during the course of his speech that under certain circumstances he would be prepared to grant
out of the Dominion treasury money to two provinces which at present had Progressive governments and to two provinces which at present had Liberal governments, but he would never consent to a dollar being paid out of the treasury of Canada to any province that had a Conservative government? Was there ever a more glaring piece of impropriety on the part of a prime minister? What does that language amount to? It is a threat or a bluff against five of the great provinces of Canada, and an inducement or a bribe to vote Liberal, and that from the lips of the Prime Minister! Surely that is "a vicious principle" to proclaim in public. It is an esqmsuire of the narrow, partisan mind of the Prime Minister himself. Language of that kind might be worthy of a Tammany leader in the lower wards of New York, where they say: You will vote the whole ticket or you will get no money; but it is unworthy falling from the lips of the Prime Minister of this country. I for one sincerely hope that for the good name of parliament, for the dignity of the house, the Prime Minister, before this debate is concluded, will rise in his place and withdraw' the improper remarks he made this afternoon.
What think you, Mr. Speaker, of the great province of Ontario, being threatened or bluffed in that manner-the richest province we have, the largest contributor in taxation to the treasury of this country, a province which recently went through a provincial election where the people, almost to the extent of eighty per cent of those who voted, cast their ballots in support of a Tory administration and returned it to power; an administration that is in office to-day by the largest majority of popular vote and sitting members that has ever existed in the Ontario legislature? What think you of a threat or a bluff to that legislature or to the voters who elected it? We provide in our election act against threats and inducements to the individual. What say we when the Prime Minister of Canada threatens a whole province that if they do not agree with him and elect a Grit legislature no money will come out of the Dominion treasury for that province?
There is another remark made this afternoon by the Prime Minister, for what purpose I know not, but a remark that I want to draw to the attention of the hon. gentleman who moved the motion. The Prime Minister argues that he has had no complaints from lawyers, doctors, professional men or financiers in regard to unemployment. Does he realize the meaning of the resolution which we are

Unemployment-Mr. Guthrie
at present discussing? It is a motion for the relief of the wage earner, not of anybody else. It is for the relief of the wage earners who are thrown out of employment. It is their cry which we hear throughout the length and breadth of the land, and it is to remedy their condition that this motion has been launched by the hon. member for North Winnipeg. I will grant that there may be room for a great difference of opinion as to what has brought about the present disastrous situation in this country. I know hon. members opposite take the view that they cannot attribute any part of this disastrous situation to the record of the present government. On the other hand I am just as firmly convinced in my own mind that the proximate cause, the chief contributing cause, of the situation which we have in Canada to-day has been the mistaken fiscal policy of this government during the years it has been in power. But let us differ upon that. We are not engaged now upon an inquiry into the causes; we are concerned with the facts. We have a situation here; or, in the language of former President Cleveland of the United States, we are confronted by a condition, not a theory. We have the unemployment, and the motion before the house asks for immediate action by way of relief.
I cannot accept the position either of the Prime Minister or of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) in regard to the responsibility which rests upon this parliament under these circumstances. I believe that, in the first instance, the liability or responsibility is upon the municipality. In the second instance, it is upon the provincial authorities. But that does not exclude liability or responsibility upon the part of this parliament. In my judgment we are legally and morally just as responsible as are the municipalities and the provinces. Let me point out just what I mean by that statement.
My hon. friend has pointed out that under the British North America Act, all charities and all eleemosynary institutions are under the control of the province. I do not think that the labouring people of this country who are out of employment are asking for charity. They are asking for rights, not for charitable contributions. I would also point out that under section 91 of the British North America Act all matters pertaining to the country at large are expressly placed under the jurisdiction of this parliament, and for those matters we are responsible. Included in them is, first, the whole question of trade and commerce. Any mismanagement of trade and commerce matters in Canada, will reflect upon employment in this country. Parliament is the only instrument that can manage or mismanage

our trade and commerce, and if we make an error which causes unemployment we surely should in the first instance bear the responsibility. Let me illustrate that by something that happened just two years ago. The then Minister of Finance brought down a measure to remove the customs duty on worsted yarns taking off the duty of 12| per cent and putting woollen yarns on the free list. Immediately after that action was taken, about 50 men were thrown out of employment in a worsted mill in the city of Guelph, and 150 were thrown out of employment in the town of Hespeler, nine miles from my city. That was the direct consequence of the action of this parliament. Nothing else intervened. This parliament decreed that worsted yarns such as were made in these factories should be placed on the free list, and no more yarns were made in those factories. They were imported from Bradford, England, and men to the number I have mentioned were thrown out of employment. AATio was responsible for that unemployment in the first instance? I do not say that that unemployment in those two individual cases exists to-day. I am using them only as an illustration of what may happen through the action of this parliament. Who caused that unemployment? Why, this Dominion parliament when it changed the tariff schedules in regard to woollen yarns.
Note, also, that the largest employers of labour in Canada are under the direct jurisdiction of this parliament; I refer to the tw'O great transportation systems. No other legislature in this country except this parliament has jurisdiction in respect to the Canadian Pacific railway or the Canadian National railway, which are by long odds the greatest employers of labour in Canada. The legislation of this parliament and of this parliament alone can affect them. We by an act, if we so chose, could throw thousands upon thousands of men out of employment on the railways. Would any responsibility rest upon us in that regard? Would not the first responsibility rest upon us in that regard? I maintain that ours would be the initial responsibility.
So, Mr. Speaker, in everything pertaining to trade and commerce and in everything pertaining to our great transportation systems we in this parliament have absolute and exclusive jurisdiction, and any act of ours that throws men out of employment surely places upon our shoulders the responsibility for anything that may occur. I cannot see it in any other light. Our responsibility for unemployment is just as great as that of the provinces and just as great as that of the municipalities. If the condition exists which I believe, nay, which I

Unemployment-Mr. Guthrie
know, exists throughout the length and breadth of Canada to-day in regard to employment and unemployment, I submit that it is our duty to intervene, and had it not been for the speech this afternoon of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, our intervention and our assistance would have been a matter of unanimous action in this house. Now that is blocked by the action of a single individual who happens for the time being to be the head of the government.
Is it too late to make a plea to the government to reconsider the position which the Prime Minister took this afternoon? I am impressed with the seriousness of the situation. I hear on every side of thousands and thousands of men out of employment. I do not get my evidence from the provincial premiers. No one needs to wait for such news; it is a matter of common knowledge. What are the conditions? Five or six thousand men out in one city in British Columbia; four hundred families in Edmonton being taken care of by the city and two hundred single men by the provincial government; ten thousand out of employment, I am told, in the city of Winnipeg; twenty-five to thirty thousand out of employment in the city of Toronto; in Windsor, thousands of mechanics walking the streets. I was in Windsor three weeks ago, and a pitiable sight is to be seen there about noon on an ordinary week day. In Oshawa thousands of men are out of employment. In every city in western Ontario it is the same story, and still the Prime Minister of this country proclaims to-day that there is no emergency, that there is nothing unusual in the situation.
The Minister of Labour, charged with the administration of the particular department which should have all the information in regard to employment and unemployment appears before us absolutely ignorant of the situation and unable to tell us how many men are to-day out of employment in the Dominion of Canada. That is the spectacle under the government of my right hon. friend, who proclaims himself a great friend of Labour. I will say this for him:	During his whole
career since 1908 in this house, I do not believe that there is any man in this country, or for that matter, in any other country, who has thought so much and has talked so much and written so much upon labour questions, and done so little for labour, as my right hon. friend. But I am not yet going to abandon all hope, I believe there is still time for him to consider the real situation. We do not need to make a party question out of this. We are not trying to gain any party advantage, notwithstanding the insinuations of the Prime Minister. It is not our motion; we were not consulted about it. There is nothing behind the motion, so far as I know, but the one	straight	question:	Shall	we	grantthe	needed	relief or	shall	we	not?
The occasions upon which I have made appeals to this government have not been very many and so far they have been uniformly unsuccessful. I wonder if I could do better on this occasion. I do not believe there is much use making an appeal under these circumstances to my hon. friend the Minister of Labour. While outwardly he is the most genial and whole-souled man you could meet anywhere, under his skin I find he is as hard as flint. I am afraid there is no hope from him. In a three hour speech he offered nothing-no remedy, no solution, no contribution, no assistance. I am afraid my appeal to him will fall on deaf ears. I see a smile on the face of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott). Is it worth my while making an appeal to him? I am afraid not. I am afraid he does not understand the real situation-he does not know what it means to have a wife and children crying for bread; if he did, I believe there would be more hope from him than from many others. Then there are my hon. friends the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) and the Minister of Railways (Mr. Crerar). No; I do not hope for much from them. Their views are circumscribed, their horizon is very limited; they cannot see past the conditions of the western wheat farmer; they know nothing of industrial employment in the rest of Canada. I am afraid I can make no impression on them. And as to my friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot), I said the Minister of Labour was hard as flint; I can only refer to the Postmaster General as harder than granite. Twice last session I tried as earnestly as a man could try, I appealed as fervently as a man could appeal, for a little more pay for the rural mail carriers, for the letter carriers, and for the railway postal clerks, and my appeal fell on deaf ears; for when I had finished he merely gave orders for the crack of the party whip and the ring of the division bells, and down I was voted.
