maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is perhaps true. I wish my hon. friend from North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) was in the house. He is a genial, smiling fellow, and I have no doubt he is a man with a big heart; he does understand the unemployment situation, and he has taken,

Unemployment-Mr. Guthrie
apparently every opportunity ito be absent during the course of this debate. He knows the condition of labour, he knows the terrible hardship of men with families to support and no money to buy food and clothing. They say that, like myself, he has a strain of good Scotch blood in him. Perhaps he is a bit thrifty, but I cannot believe it. When I recall how he was able to splash around the money of this country in North Bruce last year and is doing it again this year, I say to myself: Surely he can find in the recesses of the treasury some place where he can dig up half a million, a million or a million and a half for the relief of the unemployed at the present moment. Well, I have still my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, to appeal to. After his speech today I have not very much hope of persuading him, but I can tell him this: If he will rise to the occasion now, if he will make a compromise in the matter, if he will go down into the treasury and produce some money to assist the unemployed now, he will have the intense gratitude of a tremendous number of people in the Dominion. Some hon. members may ask why I do not do it myself. We in this house are aware that no private member can introduce a resolution or a bill involving the expenditure of one dollar of public money. That is why I am making an appeal to the government. If I were able to do so under the rules of this house, to-morrow I would bring in a bill for the expenditure of half a million, a million, or a million and a half dollars to join with the municipalities and the provinces in bearing this burden and granting this relief; but, as I say, unfortunately no private member can do so.
Now I ask my right hon. friend again if he will not do so. The bill will pass unanimously. I ask him to do it before we adjourn this Easter. Before we go home let us remedy this situation. Then while he is enjoying his Easter holiday let him develop some permanent policy to meet the recurring unemployment which comes to us annually on account of the rigour of our winter season. That is the plan I suggest to him. Do something now; that is what the motion asks-immediate action. Develop then a permanent policy and bring it down, and we will help him. I cannot imagine there is any shortage of money. Last year the government announced a surplus of 870,000,000 in the treasury. Surely there are one, or two, or three million dollars that they can devote to this laudable purpose. I cannot believe that a government that will go down into the treasury of this country and spend half a million dollars a year on motor

cars cannot dig up half a million dollars for the unemployed. I cannot believe that a government that will go down into the treasury of this country and spend half a million dollars on a building for a rich representative in the city of Washington cannot get half a million dollars for the unemployed. I tell my right hon. friend that if he tries he can get this money, and we will cause him no difficulty. Let him get it and distribute it pro rata amongst all the provinces, disregarding that improper statement which he made in the house this afternoon. Let him do it now and he will earn the gratitude of a tremendous number of people in the country now politically opposed to him. We will not oppose him, we will help him. Will he do it? He will have the unanimous voice of the House of Commons behind him if he will. I pledge myself that if he will do it I will never mention the fact as an act of contrition on his part, or a concession or admission that his government has failed to do anything during the last seven or eight years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to give to this subject of unemployment the attention that its serious character demands, and I will be a proud man if any suggestion that I may make will aid by ever so little in the solution of this question. For that reason, sir, I have neither the time nor the inclination, to imitate some of the partisan speeches that have been made in the course of this debate. Supposedly dealing with unemployment they were very much earmarked as being part of the usual preelection political ballyhoo-I think that is the word. As the debate progressed I recognized the time-worn platitudes, the glistening generalities, and the old familiar catchwords that we associate with the approach of a general election. Let me quote some of them: Canada the land of promise; Canada the land of broad, wide open spaces; our red-blooded citizens; the hand that rocks the cradle rules the world, and so on; but often descending to the most petty personalities, both as regards parties and as regards individuals.
Now, what aid is it to the unemployed if we say that Bob on one side of the house, after hours of debate, demonstrates that Peter on the other side once upon a time made a political bet; or we will say that Jim on this side of the house, after much wrangling of Hansard and so on, proves that John on the other side three weeks ago at some place in the west, said something somewhat different from the language he used when opening a flower show in Prince Edward Island nine and

Unemployment-Mr. Neill
three quarter years before? That is the sort of stuff we have been listening to. Is this the best statesmanship we can give to the men who sent us here? If we cannot act as statesmen at least let us try to reach a little higher grade than schoolboys squabbling over a game of marbles.
Now, as regards the unemployment question, I want to state my position quite frankly. I am of the opinion that the Dominion government, being the dominant factor, so to speak, in the confederation of the provinces should call a conference of the provinces to deal with this subject. I think the conference should have a twofold purpose in mind. First, it should discuss the underlying causes of more or less permanent or recurring unemployment, and the possible remedies for those conditions. Secondly, in a subordinate degree, it should consider with the provinces unemployment insurance, and whether they could cooperate either to devise a scheme that would be workable under the British North America Act as it now exists, or, with the consent of all the provinces, make such a change in the British North America Act as would permit the inauguration of such a scheme. The idea of such a conference would meet with general support throughout the country. It would not commit the government to any lavish expenditure, beyond preliminary expenses, and much good would be likely to come from it. It would perhaps demonstrate to our industries methods of reducing seasonal unemployment, which is so much a cause of the trouble. It would educate us in the true conditions regarding the unemployment situation.
May I say a word at this point in regard to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon. I think he misapprehended the purpose and the meaning of the amendment introduced by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). The amendment is that in the opinion of this house the government should take immediate action to deal with the question of unemployment. That is the amendment, and no more than that. The Prime Minister appeared to go upon the premises that his government had been asked to make two very heavy expenditures, one to meet immediate relief and the other to inaugurate a system of unemployment insurance. Neither is an essential of the request made in the resolution. In the first instance, as to dealing with unemployment, it might take the form of a reduction of expenses. For instance, it might be asked or suggested that immigration should be curtailed, and a saving thereby effected, or it
might necessitate certain legislation or representations to encourage industry to cut down periods of seasonal unemployment. At this stage I might quote a clipping from to-night's issue of a labour paper in the United States:
Governor Roosevelt, of New York state, has appointed a committee of five to study and make plans for the stabilization of industry and the prevention of unemployment.
This has nothing to do with the present depression, but is looking forward to the preventing of a recurrence of unemployment in the future. That is what I understood the purpose of the amendment before us to be. As to unemployment insurance, the resolution does not ask, and the government might never be asked, to spend a nickel in connection with it. It may be found when this conference is called that the provinces will be agreeable to recognizing unemploymeift as their responsibility, and they might agree to pay the whole of the State's share of unemployment insurance. However, as no one province can successfully inaugurate a system of unemployment relief, and it would be impossible to have nine different and competing systems, it would be necessary for the Dominion government to inaugurate what might be called the machinery, and the different provinces would come in and agree to bear the expense. Possibly it has been suggested that the Dominion government might pay a portion, but it does not follow as a matter of course that because we ask the Dominion Government to consider legislation of that nature we are asking it to commit itself to any outlay in that regard.
As to unemployment, I am afraid as long as we have our present economic conditions, and the easy way in which we can speed up production, we will always have it with us; I think it will get worse. Even when times are thoroughly prosperous there is a great amount of unemployment, as I shall attempt to show in a moment. Then when the reaction comes the drop from the high standard of employment makes it even more severe. I am inclined to agree with a leading economist of the United States who says that unemployment will be the biggest problem in that country during the next decade, and he attributes the condition to standardization of industry and to improved technique. To bring it home to us in Canada, I shall quote the conditions in Vancouver. If I understood correctly the hon. member who just took his seat, he said that in one city of the province of British Columbia there are between five thousand and six thousand unemployed. No doubt when he quotes those figures he is exercising a political poetic licence, because, I have returns from Vancouver, the big-
Unemployment-Mr. Neill

gest city of British Columbia, to the effect that for the two weeks ending January 29, 1930, there were only 1,093 unemployed. It cost that city $25,400 for those two weeks to furnish work for unemployed labour. For total relief including people who were not able to work, the cost was $36,000. For the whole of last year the total cost for unemployment work and relief in the city of Vancouver was $232,000. This condition is coincident with a period of prosperity in that city. The industrial payroll has gone up $1,700,000 in the last year; more than one thousand men have been added to the industrial payroll in the city of Vancouver, and it is in a prosperous condition, the total payroll being $65,000,000 a year. Yet we have a constantly growing number of unemployed who require assistance.
I had occasion recently to took at these men; I went out and watched them at work. I did not announce myself or speak to the foreman, but I just watched them, and I wish to say that only a very small percentage of those men were apparently addicted to either drink or dope. They were not the down-and-out variety, but were honest working men, quite able, willing and anxious to work if they could. I watched the rate at which they worked and I found it was up to the average. I must say that they worked a good deal harder than I would have done for one dollar a day; the single man receives one dollar per day, and the married man two dollars.
Early in the month of January the city of Vancouver called an unemployment conference. That city invited a representative from the Dominion government, which did not send one and should have done so; it invited representatives from the province, who acted in a similar manner to the Dominion; it invited the British Columbia provincial members and all the Dominion members from the province of British Columbia. As a result one of the provincial members attended, and none of the federal members, except myself. I had three days' travel to get there and back, whereas many members who lived in the city of Vancouver or nearby did not attend; probably they did not have the time or interest to go and inquire into the industrial and unemployment conditions in their own locality. I venture to say they will find an abundance of time, however, during the next election campaign to come swarming into my constituency as they have done in the past in a method comparable only to the nine plagues in the time of the Pharaohs, seeking, of course, to coerce and bully the electorate, and to compel them to vote in such a way as to suit their peculiar points of view. I am 
glad to say my electors are free born, independent men and women, and not coerced so easily.
I may say, indeed, that the invasion has already begun. Last week a cabinet minister and a private member of the legislature took part in a nominating convention in my district, and the Hon. R. L. (Pat) Maitland was quoted as saying this:
Speaking of Independent candidates, Mr. Maitland said that he had never met Mr. Neill. He must be a good man or he would not occupy his present position.
I have often had occasion to applaud remarks made by our Conservative friends, but I do not think I have ever done it with more sincerity than when I applaud that remark. I hope he will come again and bring his friends with him. If they follow the line this man took it will do me good, and if they take a different line it will do them harm.
At this conference on unemployment I was asked to say a few words, and I pointed out at that time what I thought were the underlying causes and possible remedies. I am glad to say since I have come to this house I learn from the remarks made by labour and other members that my views coincide a good deal with theirs. The suggested causes of unemployment which I gave were four: First, over-immigration; second, seasonal production and unregulated production; third, the mechanization of industry, which is even extending to farming now, and fourth, business depression. Possibly that last is more caused by unemployment, but there are cases in which financial panics, stock market crashes and the like, would affect employment.
The remedies which I suggested, in a simple way, were: First, with regard to immigration, my suggestion was to stop assisted immigration. That has been generally accepted by the country and I understand the government has put it more or less into effect, but I will go further and suggest that we stop all immigration for the present time. We have a precedent for that in New Zealand, which is very much in touch with the old country. I saw recently, on February 1, that Sir Joseph Ward, the Prime Minister of New Zealand, stated that he has notified Great Britain that owing to the number of unemployed in New Zealand his government would not be able to accept any of Great Britain's surplus population. If that is good for New Zealand probably it would be good for us, for a short time at least.
Then I would suggest that the Dominion government, the provincial governments and the municipalities take active steps so to

Unemployment-Mr. Neill
arrange their programs of expenditure-because they spend enormous sums of money in the aggregate-as to make the work begin earlier in the spring and continue until later in the fall. Certainly that would help a great deal in keeping down the peak of employment, and would result in a smaller number being unemployed in the winter time. Then again I think industry should be encouraged by the government, and perhaps by the provinces as well, to aid in doing away with rush periods. I am not familiar with the boot and shoe business, but I am told that there is a period, three or four months in length and occurring twice a year, in which the peak production is reached, after which there is a slack time. Probably that could be overcome. There is an industry in the United States dealing with some foreign product which enters that country only about three months in the year. That formerly meant an enormous difference between the high and low levels of employment, something like 600 per cent. Now they are putting this product into cold storage for a while, and that has brought that difference down to normal. It is good business for them to make that change, because now they have permanent, steady workmen in their service. Things like that would cost nothing and would help industry, and the different branches of industry might be encouraged along that line by means of investigations by government officials or possibly by a commission appointed for that purpose. I can illustrate that point by referring again to the commission appointed by Governor Roosevelt of the state of New York, which has for its purpose the readjustment of industry to reduce seasonal unemployment.
Then we come to the question of the mechanization of industry. Of course it is obvious what that means. Production by machinery has gone ahead so fast that to-day one man can produce what it used to take ten, twenty, or thirty men to produce. Not only is that the case, but we have also constant new inventions. Hardly a month, and certainly not a year, goes by without comparatively large bodies of men not only being thrown out of work temporarily but finding their occupation entirely wiped out owing to the invention of some improved machinery. These are things we cannot avoid and could not stop. We would not stop them if we could; that would be going back to medieval times, like doing away with trains and so on, but we should take cognizance of it and take steps to remedy any grievance or any hardship which might result from this rapid increase in mechanization.
Now we come to the last remedy which I suggest both for these and for other conditions which I have outlined. I suppose it will be regarded as revolutionary, but my suggestion is that we should have a shorter working day. I was much surprised and pleased to hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) state during the course of his remarks that there had been a petition signed by the mayor and council, on behalf of the citizens of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba, asking that the Dominion government take steps to shorten the working day. If a city council as large as that of Winnipeg, composed for the most part, not of working men but of business men, can take that line, surely it is worth at least considering, and it shows that such a movement possibly might be acceptable generally. I see that the Labour Statesman, of Vancouver, endorses the same idea and says:
While the short-sighted employers of Canada desire an ever abundant supply of subsidized immigrants, so that they can continue to operate their industries with low-paid labour, from everywhere there is the cry for more markets to consume the products of the modern producing machine. What better way is there than to make this possible by a well-paid wageearning class?
Certainly I can endorse that suggestion.
Now we come to the question of unemployment insurance, and I put that last because I realize that it is only a palliative, that it is only treating a symptom of the disease. It is like a doctor treating a man for a headache when he has a fever. It is all right to treat the symptom but at the same time you must get at the underlying trouble. Here I differ for the first time, I think, with my hon. friend for North Winnipeg. He says the Dominion can and should and must deal with the question, that it is our responsibility as members of this federal parliament. Well, the Scriptures say that if you have faith you may move mountains, but it does not say anything about faith moving the British North America Act. If I have enough 60 per cent dynamite I can remove the mountain without, faith, but I can do nothing with the British North America Act. I may say that to-day is some other day in the month or year than the calendar shows it to be, but no amount of eloquence and no amount of belief on my part can change the cold fact that it is not that day. It is just the same with the British North America Act; no matter how much we may desire that the government should not be bound by that act, the fact remains that the government is bound, and we cannot evade that fact.
Unemployment-Mr. Neill

Let me quote an instance which comes from British Columbia. Ever since the time of confederation the government has proceeded on the theory that the fisheries were entirely under the jurisdiction of the Dominion. A case came up in police court; it was appealed and went on from court to court until finally it went to the privy council, where it was decided that a considerable proportion of the jurisdiction, that on land, belongs to the provinces. What is the condition? That does not suit the Dominion; it does not suit the provinces either and certainly it does not suit the industry, because it is a dual control which is undesirable, but what are we to do about it? We say it is wrong, that the Dominion should have complete control. I will agree with that. Some people think the provinces should have the entire responsibility, but they do not have it. That is the British North America Act, and that is an illustration that no matter how much we may desire to get away from that act, we cannot do so. Change it if you like; get together with the provinces and agree to amend it, but we cannot ignore it.
The hon. member spoke of old age pensions as an example of what this government could do. That is an entirely different thing. In connection with old age pensions we gave the provinces so much money and we did not propose to force the working man to pay a portion of his wages as would be the case if we had unemployment insurance. I need not go into that; it is obvious that one province could not successfully inaugurate an unemployment insurance scheme. I grant that the Dominion could and perhaps should assist; I do not know about that; they can assist if all the provinces are agreeable, but if all the provinces are agreeable you can do anything; you can change the British North America Act if you like.
Now I want to refer to the report with respect to unemployment insurance brought to the house last year by the committee on industrial and international relations. The committee recommended simply that the federal government be requested to bring the subject matter of the report before the next Dominion-provincial conference. I find that the Ottawa Journal of the next day has this to say, after commenting on the report:
It is to be hoped that parliament and the government find a resting place for these recommendations in the most convenient waste basket.
. ... It is absolute nonsense. This country has no more need of unemployment insurance than it has need of polygamy.
I wonder what the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) thinks about that 
statement in his party organ. That was not published thirty or forty years ago; that was last year. It reminds me of an item which appeared in a newspaper many years ago with regard to a man who was trying to sell shares in a telephone company. The newspaper said he should be put in gaol, because everybody knew it was nonsense and even if it could be used there was no commercial value in itl Times change, however, and there has been a considerable feeling growing up throughout the country with regard to this question even in the last year. We find three large cities in Canada suggesting this same thing, and then we have the resolution referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson) passed by this convention on unemployment held recently in Winnipeg. This convention was not composed of unemployed men, but rather of representatives of cities, men in business who were responsible for the financing and running of those cities. This convention passed a resolution which concluded as follows:
Therefore be it resolved that this conference endorses the principle of unemployment insurance, and urges the calling of an interprovincial and federal conference at the earliest possible date for the consideration of the adoption of a Dominion-wide scheme.
The mover of that resolution was an aider-man from Fort William, not a working man in the sense of being unemployed, and the seconder was a representative of the Saskatchewan government. As I have pointed out already, that was not a council of idle men, it was a conference of business men seeking a solution for this problem.
I would like to emphasize that when we speak of unemployment insurance we do not mean the dole. The dole has been mixed up with unemployment insurance, much to the disadvantage of this insurance scheme. This insurance is similar to that carried on by fraternal societies, where the insured must have paid for thirteen weeks before he can collect anything and where he can draw only so much per year. The government of the day in Great Britain, perhaps owing to some pressure of politics, or I believe some strike, put down the bars and extended the benefits. The result was not an insurance, it was a payment to all and sundry who asked for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is it not a fact that in Great Britain the employees have to subscribe to the fund when they are in employment?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, but under the extended system they were released from having to make any payments before getting relief. Beginning, I think, on May 1, they are going

Unemployment-Mr. Macdougall
back to the old system. It will then pay its way, as it did before they introduced the extended system known as the dole. The trades and labour council has gone on record as being in favour of this scheme. I will not detain the house by reading their resolution, but they are in favour of the workmen paying at least one-third of the cost, and the scheme being put on an actuarial basis.
I believe that public sentiment is veering towards this proposed scheme. When a city the size of Vancouver is forced to pay more than a quarter of a million dollars annually for relief, is it any wonder that they are interested in a reasonable system of unemployment insurance. The question of cost is always a vital one. The suggestion is that a third is to be paid b3^ the men, a third by the employers, and a third by the state, although it is not stated whether that is dominion or provincial, or whether that third will be split half and half. But in the consideration of this phase of cost we should not overlook the concealed cost.
Unfortunately, unemployment is progressive. Every man who is out of employment is forced to butt into the other man's job, and that throws him out. Then presently he and his family have lost their purchasing power, and that in turn throws more men out of employment. A considerable loss is brought about by deterioration. Six weeks' idleness makes a man a potential hobo; six months' idleness makes him a potential criminal. In the early nineties I had an experience in the city of Vancouver somewhat along that line. I was very hard up, and could not get work, although I had not reached the point of actual destitution, but I could not help but notice the rapid mental degeneration of other men in like circumstances. The idle rich can find something with which to employ themselves, but the idle poor has nothing to do. A man in such circumstances deteriorates mentally and physically at a most remarkable and rapid gait. Three years ago I was in the House of Commons in London and I heard a man who is now a member of the cabinet make the statement that ithe gap between unemployed and unemployable was very narrow, and that the gap between unemployable and criminal was narrower still. A man will steal before he will see his children starve, at least I know I would. Think what is involved in that. We are forced to pay the cosits of an army of police, courts, magistrates, judges, jails and such things. Statisticians tell us that after a man has been in jail three times he rarely comes back; he is a criminal for the rest of his life, and has to be kept by the people. If he has
been in jail twice, he has some hope, and that hope is increased where he has had but one jail sentence. A certain percentage of the men sent to jail for petty stealing into which they are forced by these conditions will never get back to normal life. Then there is the price of ill health to be paid. Statisticians tell us that preventable ill health costs more than all the wars in the world. Wars occur only occasionally, but this thing is going on all the time. There is a lack of proper sanitation, a lack of proper food and clothing; all these things tell upon the population. There are the mental, moral and physical weaklings caused by such conditions, who in turn breed further generations of weaklings.
Unemployment insurance is insurance not only against unemployment but against something else-it is insurance against sovietism. I do not say that the working man of Canada would go to that extreme, he has too much sense, but we must be prepared to meet the political upheaval which might follow a continuance of such conditions. How can we assume that a starving man or woman will reason with the precision of a university professor? Can we blame them for acts committed when they are in a condition of helplessness and hopelessness. I do not know of two more damnable conditions in which the human mind can ;be than those of absolute hopelessness and absolute helplessness. Can we wonder that men in such a state of mind will hit out against the system under which they are suffering and under which they do not receive a fair deal?
Deducting these costs from any monetary costs of establishing a system of unemployment insurance leaves a very small debit, if any, to be considered. The question is not that we cannot afford to do it, but that we cannot afford not to do it. It is our duty as would-be statesmen working for the people to do everything possible to not only check this continual unemployment but to relieve any occasional unemployment which may still occur.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I trust that the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Neill) will not adjudge me guilty of any lack of courtesy if I do not attempt to follow his remarks. I do not do so for the reason that the hon. member, like myself, is a private member, and the responsibility for this matter rests upon the government. I would refer to the speech of the man to whom the labouring people of Canada have looked during this debate, namely the man in control of the Labour department, the Minister of Labour (Mr. 1254	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Macdougall
Heenan). Before I make any comments upon his remarks, may I offer him perhaps what is a unique form of congratulation? I have to congratulate him for delivering in this House of Commons what in my judgment was certainly one of the longest, one of the most illogical, one of the most inelegantly expressed, and one of the most hopelessly mixed speeches ever inflicted upon any parliament of Canada. Out of this Gratiano performance of the Minister of Labour, I shall attempt to extract some little common sense. I use that character as an example, because when Shakespeare delineated the character of Gratiano in the Merchant of Venice there must have passed through the prophetic mind of the great poet a performance such as we had yesterday from the Minister of Labour. Certainly the minister spoke an infinite deal of nothing; his reasons were as two grains of wheat hid in two bushels of chaff; you shall seek all day ere you find them, and when you have them, they are not worth the search.
Out of this welter of illogical conclusions and grammatical errors I have tried to extract a little common sense. I have found this: the hon gentleman told us in his speech that he had conceived a permanent plan to solve unemployment in Canada; he had conceived that within the fathomless-I had almost said abyss, but I will say recesses-of his mighty mind. It has not been given to the people of Canada yet. I could very well conjure up the sleepless nights and laborious hours that the hon. gentleman consumed in evolving the plan within his mind. I could very well understand the amount of mental energy that was consumed in the process that he described. But after telling us that he had devoted all this time to forming some plan to deal with unemployment in this country, he wasted two hours of the time of the house in reading extracts trying to prove that there was no unemployment to which the great plan that he had endeavoured to evolve could be applied. I mention this just to indicate one of the choice illogical titbits from the clumsy and spavined intellectual performance of my hon. friend.
Ah, but there is, in the speech of my hon. friend, another point, if I may so designate it to which I should like to refer. Not, mark you, saying what he said in London; not saying what he will say in the back concessions when he is let loose from parliament, he said that the time was not yet ripe for unemployment insurance. Why? Because, he says, the people of this country have to be educated; it is advanced social legislation and the working people have to be educated before we can

introduce unemployment insurance. Whence must their education come? We would naturally suppose it would come from the man who presides over the destinies of the Labour department for the whole of Canada. If that be the fountain head, the source whence education on this problem of unemployment insurance must come, all I have to say to the unemployed, to the organized labouring people of Canada is this:	The Minister of Labour
is the source whence education on unemployment insurance must come: read his speech and then weep for yourselves, for your children and for unemployment insurance.
But there might be some point in having public opinion in Canada crystallized along the line of unemployment insurance. If there be any need for education along this line, the party that now holds power has had ample opportunity in which to provide it. I read over the platform on which the Prime Minister attained his position as leader of the Liberal party, on which he succeeded in getting the votes of the electorate, and I find that in that platform was a commission for unemployment insurance. That was in 1919, eleven years ago. What did the Prime Minister have to say about it this afternoon? Did he come out and say, as I suppose he would say when he accepted nomination as leader of the party, that he would do something? In all the ramblings of the Prime Minister this afternoon you cannot find a single definite, positive statement, that he is going to do anything in regard to the question of unemployment insurance. Yet he was able, supporting unemployment insurance as one of the planks in his platform, to get the votes of the people of this country. Fortunate it is for the people, particularly for the unemployed, that he will never get those votes again! But if there be any education required in regard to the matter of unemployment insurance- and I want to submit this to the Minister of Labour that labour in Canada will not take kindly to that suggestion; for labour in Canada is just as advanced in the matter of social problems as labour in any other country in the world. They do not need any education, particularly from the Minister of Labour. He is not capable of giving any education to anybody. But eleven years have passed since the Prime Minister adopted this plank in the Liberal party and nothing has been done.
There is in the speech of the Minister of Labour another statement to which I might make a passing reference. He said that the present government should be given great credit for the fact that it is going to establish an eight-hour day on public works under

Unemployment-Mr. Macdougall
government control. May I point this out? For two years the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), myself and others in the opposition have been demanding that this be done. Last year when the minister's estimates were before the house, we succeeded in getting a promise from him that he would at this session introduce a bill making provision for an eight-hour day on works controlled by the government of Canada, and also making provision for the payment of a living wage. When there was no sign of that bill being introduced in the early stages of this session, at the very first occasion on which the Minister of Public Works introduced his estimates, I took the matter up again and for over an hour discussed it in the house. Two weeks afterwards, when nothing was being done, members of the opposition, including myself, held up the estimates of the Minister of Public Works for two hours and a half until we succeeded in getting a definite promise that that legislation would be introduced at the present session. It is now being introduced, and one of the Toronto papers, I think it was the Toronto Star, supporting the present government, comes out with the statement that this legislation will mean $600,000 a year to the people of Canada. They follow this with the statement: "Hats off to Peter Heenan."

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I hear some members faintly applauding. I hope they will applaud after I have concluded my statement. I might point out that the hon. gentleman to whom hats ought to be taken off has been Minister of Labour for four years. I think he assumed office in 1926; he should never have assumed it at all. If that legislation which he was forced by the opposition to bring into the house means $600,000 a year to labour in this country, this means simply that the hon. gentleman by his passivity and indifference to the cause of labour for four years has brought about a loss to labour amounting to $2,400,000, on account of his not having introduced that legislation four years ago. Let the Toronto Daily Star take account of that statement, and then let it give it out to the labour people of Canada and ask them to take their hats off to the Minister of Labour. So much for the rambling, rattling, illogical speech of the Minister of Labour.
In respect to the amendment which is before the house, there is no other question that could be considered by the parliament of Canada which is of greater importance
than that of unemployment. Not only is this question serious to those men-and there are to-day thousands of them in Canada- who stand idle, who are without work, whose wives and children as a consequence are without bread, but it is a matter of very great consequence and concern to the whole of society. Society has been compared by sociologists to the human body. Just as the human body is made of different members, so too is society. Individuals are the members of society. Where, in the case of the human body, its members are functioning properly, you have a healthy physical organism. Where one or two members may not be functioning properly, you have a diseased organism. So too, in the case of society. Where you have hundreds of thousands unemployed-and there are over a hundred thousand unemployed in Canada today, although the Minister of Labour evidently does not know anything about it- where you have that vast number without work and their dependents starving, you have a situation that affects not only the individuals immediately concerned but the whole of society.
Now I come to the argument of the right hon. the Prime Minister. It is this, that unemployment should be a question first for the individual; secondly, for the family; then for the municipality; then for the province; and then, I suppose, as a natural consequence, because he could not escape responsibility any further, it becomes a matter for the Dominion government. Speaking on the address in this house the Prime Minister said that unemployment was first a question for the individual, and then for the family. 1 do not think that I ever listened to a more absurd statement falling from the lips of any public man. What did he mean when he said' that? There is only one conclusion, and that is that he meant that unemployment was a question to be solved by the individual who is unemployed. In other words, he propounds to the unemployed people of Canada this choice morsel of sophistry, that unemployment should be the problem of the unemployed and should be paid for by them. If there was any sense at all in his remarks, that is the only sense that I could extract from them.

Hansard, in the Prime Minister's speech on the address. My right hon. friend does not get me on that kind of thing; I come armed with the reference. Just look it up. I wish to

say to the right hon. gentleman that I entirely disagree with him when he says that the first body that is responsible in this matter is the municipality, and then the province.
Let us see why it was that men formed themselves into societies. We have, first, the society which we call the home, where members are drawn together by propinquity and ties of blood. Later they join together in municipalities, and then in provinces, and then, in the case of this country, the provinces joined together in one dominion. Why did they do that? They did it for the purpose of securing for the individual citizen greater security and protection. There is no question about that; it is the only reason for the formation of the Canadian confederation. That is the only reason why the provinces joined together in order to form this great dominion. They did it because they wanted to be sure that in times of stress and need, when the individual was in difficult straits, they would have a powerful social organization behind them to help them out.
But there is another consideration. I wish to point out to this house that when this dominion was formed, the various provincial governments gave up to this central power, this power which is supposed above all others to protect them, the majority of their sources of taxation. The provinces retain only the sources of direct taxation, and even those sources, I submit, have been invaded by the present government and by previous federal governments. I mention the income tax as an illustration. We must in discussing these problems extract some canon of social justice. What is the canon that must be extracted here? The canon in the application of matters of this kind is that the strongest back shall bear the heaviest burden. Whose back is the strongest as between the federal provincial and municipal bodies? In 1867, when this dominion was formed, Ontario-I might take any other province-was receiving a revenue from duties amounting to only $2,000,000. In 1929, the government over which the right hon. Prime Minister presides took from the people of the province of Ontario in duties, $103,000,000. And so with the other provinces. The federal government has invaded the provincial sources of revenue. The federal government is capable of dealing with situations such as unemployment throughout the country, and from the very organization of society it is absolutely logical and absolutely just that the federal government should deal with a situation such as unemployment.
We have had a lot of loose talk in this house about the British North America Act

and about the powers of the provincial and federal governments. I want to ask this question of the Prime Minister. Perhaps he may not answer me at all; I do not suppose he will. Is there anything in the British North America Act to prevent this government giving assistance to the provinces to help relieve unemployment ?

I do not wish to detract at all from the literary and economic efforts of my right hon. friend. I may say that before I ever came to this parliament I had read thrice the book from which he quoted this afternoon. To my mind it was excellent. It did credit to the right hon. gentleman who occupies the exalted position of Prime Minister. In some respects it has distinct literary merits. But though it is a good book to read, extracts from it are very poor feeding for the unemployed people of Canada. In the Scriptures we read of people who were crying for bread and were offered a stone. Well, the right hon. Prime Minister is not quite that bad. But what do the unemployed get from the Prime Minister when they send a delegation here composed of representatives from all over the country? And, Mr. Speaker, that to my mind is the most humiliating spectacle the people of Canada have ever had to witness-men in this great, young, rich country to have to come here to beg for bread! What did they get from the right hon. Prime Minister? They got ringing, jingling, platitudinous sentences from Industry and Humanity, and they are supposed to go back satisfied with that treatment. He had to admit to-night that there is nothing in the constitution to prevent him

Now, I say to the right hon. He said: "The letter killeth but the spirit giveth life." He stated that he would not contribute to assist unemployment in the provinces where the governments are not Liberal. But, Mr. Speaker, this question is one that transcends party politics. My right hon. friend after reading those very beautiful extracts from Industry and Humanity, with all the idealism which he had conjured up during his residence in the United States, fell down to-day.

In this book which is so beautifully phrased, Industry and Humanity, and in which he expresses such high ideals, he tells us what he was prepared to do for labour in this country, and having quoted extract after extract, five minutes afterwards he says in effect-and I think it was the most disgraceful statement I ever listened to in this house-

speechtext:
All right, I will
change the adjective and say the most humiliating spectacle I ever saw, and the most humiliating pronouncement that I ever heard in this house-he said in effect: that although women and children were starving in this country he would not contribute out of the abundant revenues of this Dominion five cents to keep them alive, if the government of the province in which they were starving happened to be politically different from the right hon. gentleman. I think he had better write an appendix to Industry and Humanity after making that statement.
Well now. with all this cant, with all this drivel about constitutional objections, I want to say to my right hon. friend to-night, first of all, there is nothing in the constitution that will prevent him from helping the unemployed, to save them from starving; and certainly there is nothing in the constitution to prevent the provinces from receiving grants from this government for that purpose. But I want to add, he has a responsibility in this connection, for the simple reason that the unemployment existing in the Dominion today, and it is very general, exists because of the failure of the government over which he presides. Nationally considered, there are four factors in the matter of national productivity; they are, first, land-I use the term in its economic sense to include not only the surface of the earth, but all the resources with which we have been endowed by ProvifM Mackenzie King,]
dence: second, labour; third, capital, in the sense of capital goods; fourth, the managerial ability which must come from the government that controls the destiny of the state.
Now, let us see if in respect to any or all of these factors they have fallen down. Can anyone say we have unemployment because our natural resources are not sufficient to provide a good living for our sparse population?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen
say "no". I am glad to hear that. Undoubtedly to-day we have illimitable opportunities for the production of wealth, we have potential wealth of .farm, forest, sea and mine. We should be able to provide a good living in this country not only for ten million people but for one hundred million people, and we could do so if we had a proper government. Consequently I say to this house to-night that the first factor to be considered in the matter of national competition has not fallen down. We cannot blame Providence for stinting in the matter of bestowing natural resources upon this great young country.
Let us take the second factor, that of labour. Does any man in this house, whether he be Grit, Tory or Progressive, mean to tell me that the men who stand idle to-day, the men to whom the Prime Minister directed his platitudes in his sentences from Industry and Humanity this afternoon, do so because it is a pleasure to them to be idle? Do they desire to see their wives and little children starving? On behalf of the labourers of this country I want to say that all they want is the opportunity to work at fair wages. Consequently, the second factor in national productive enterprise has not fallen down.
Thirdly, we come to the factor of capital. With our great natural resources there should be no difficulty whatever, were it not for the unwise fiscal policy of this government, to get all the capital we want in order to develop the abundant natural resources with which we have been endowed by a bountiful Providence. There is no reason why we should not have all the capital we want.
If the first three factors have not fallen down, what has fallen down? I will tell you. The thing that has fallen down is the directive force which those factors must and should receive from the right hon. Prime Minister and those hon. members who are associated with him. There can be no doubt about that. How can we expect to have anything but unemployment in this country when we have promulgated and supported by this govern-

Unemployment-Mr. Irvine
ment policy which is not Canadian but one under which raw materials of Canada are shipped, formed and fashioned in American mills and factories, by American workmen? What can we expect in Canada, other than unemployment, when the only solicitude that this government is capable of providing is to fill the factories with American workmen? I am not speaking too strongly on this subject.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, I am not speaking too strongly; I am speaking very fairly, and if any evidence is needed to prove that statement it can be readily found in the trade returns between this country and the United States of America. During the last year we brought in from the United States over $900,000,000 worth of goods. We had an unfavourable trade balance with our great southern neighbour of $347,000,000. Seventy-five per cent of those goods could have been produced in Canada by Canadian workmen, and if they had been produced here we could have given employment to 500,000 Canadian people. We have in this country to-day about 100,000 unemployed. Not only is it necessary that we should have a wise fiscal policy, but if the right hon. gentleman who tells us he never resided in the United States would think a little more in terms of Canada than in terms of the American republic, we would have our people working. It would affect not only the 100,000 people who are now fed in the soup kitchens of this country, to the great disgrace not of Canada but of the Canadian government, but it would affect also 400,000 other Canadians who are endeavouring to find employment in this country.
The other day my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Cantley) stated that there is coming into this country each day $1,000,000 worth of steel and steel products. Eighty per cent of those products could be manufactured in Canadian steel mills; why are they not manufactured here? The reason is that we have a government in Canada that is legislating not so much in the interests of Canada as in the interests of the republic to the south. It is time for someone in Canada to speak up about this condition. When you speak about it, however, you are hushed by the Prime Minister. He will tell us that we must not provoke the United States, even to the extent of giving up the livelihood of Canadian men and women. I admire the great republic to the south, and I seek no ground to disagree with them. I say, however, that when young men in public life in this country-
