maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I wish to read once again the amendment which is before the house. Although it has been read by several hon. members, I wish to make special reference to the inference drawn by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), namely, that the amendment necessarily involves a large expenditure of money. It is quite clear that the terms of the motion do not justify that inference. With that in mind I shall read it once more. It was moved by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) and seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland):
That in the opinion of this house the government should take immediate action to deal with the question of unemployment.
There may be many ways of " dealing " with unemployment without expending public money. That is for the government to discover.
I have been amazed at the amount of heat which has developed in this discussion, and with few exceptions I have been amazed equally by the lack of light. I was surprised that the saintly, peace-loving Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) should have injected a note of antagonism in his reply to the argument of the hon. member for North Winnipeg. Certainly he did not hold true to his title of peacemaker when he opened this debate by baiting the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) and by placing the whole discussion on a low, narrow partisan basis. I am interested in this question of unemployment because it is the most outstanding indication of the disintegration which is taking place in modern civilization. I am interested in it, moreover, from the point of view of a student; above all I am interested in it because of its human implications. Because of my interest in the matter from these points of view I deplore the attitude taken by hon. members in this discussion. Unquestionably there has been an effort on the part of some hon. gentlemen to extract political advantage from the tragic condition we have been trying to discuss. I should think the hon. members who have tried to do that have indicated that they are more skilled in political strategy than they are in economics. If hon. members of this house were to get their deserts for their failure to cope with the vital problem now before us I fear, Mr. Speaker, that very few of us would come back after the next election.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
" Speak for yourself, John."

Unemployment-Mr. Irvine

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, I am speaking for myself also in this regard, for I must acknowledge, with other men who have been entrusted with public office, that the question of unemployment has represented so far the bankruptcy of statesmanship throughout the civilized world. If you will permit me to call myself a statesman of the bankruptcy type, I must line myself up with all the others and say: "We have failed to find a solution for the problem.''
Catch phrases suitable for winning elections never have been noted for their achievements 'n settling matters of great economic importance. Our consumers' league across the way, with their fine phrases about free trade, find that the problem has escaped them; hon. gentlemen to my right, with their phrases about higher protection, are not touching the problem either. Even a greater party, in my opinion, than either of the two parties in this house, the Labour party of Great Britain, seems to have gone to seed also on the catchword of public ownership, thinking that would be a solution. Unfortunately, up to this point even that great government has not found much of a solution for unemployment.
I want to support the resolution, Mr. Speaker, because it deals with a question that confronts not only Canada but the entire civilized world to-day, a question which is ominous and one for which a solution must be found or civilization itself will succumb. Then I want to support also the suggestion of the hon. member who moved the resolution that, as a tentative thing, giving assistance to those who are suffering at the present time from the evils of unemployment, a system of unemployment insurance should be introduced. I agree that that is a tentative thing; it is temporary, something to be carried on until we have found a solution for the problem. While there is no better solution I agree that this should be done. In the absence of that better way, to which I have referred, I should say that unemployment insurance is an imperative need in Canada today, as it is in other countries.
Surely unemployment will be taken as a fact without any wealth of figures to demonstrate it. To argue in this house that there is such a thing as unemployment and to back up that argument with copious figures, seems to me analogous to an attempt to prove that the world is round, quoting once again the old arguments which support that view. I think unemployment is a fact as well established in the minds of the people of the country to-day as is the physical fact of the shape of the planet on which we live. It is a fact which bears with it some problems which are

grim, ugly and ominous. Indeed, unemployment is no longer confined merely to the wage earners. Of course we always have had an unemployed rich class; they are still with us, only they are a little more fortunate than the other unemployed. They can live on interest, but the unemployed at the other end of the social order cannot live on nothing.
There are intellectual workers in the ranks of the unemployed. Our public school system with its easier access to institutions of secondary education is overstocking the market in the professional world. Lawyers, doctors and teachers, while they may not be actually lined up in the ranks of the unemployed, are finding it more and more difficult to get employment at fair remuneration in the work to which they have devoted their lives and their study. We also have industries unemployed, with millions of dollars' worth of machinery tied up, rusting, and doing nothing. There you have unemployment of a kind which will appeal to hon. members of this house.
As I say, unemployment is not confined to one class; it is becoming more and more not only an acute problem but one that is widespread. It is the most prominent symptom of a civilization which is in the process of disintegration. How far that disintegration will go, no one knows; whether intelligence will arrest this disintegration and gather together the decaying pieces remains yet to be seen. I think it was H. G. Wells who remarked in this connection that civilization was in a great race between intelligence and disaster. Judging from the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Labour I would be inclined to bet on disaster winning the race; if we are to depend upon the labour leader of this country; if his utterances may be taken as indicative of his views and his activity in this matter; if we are to take that as the leadership of Canada on a question of this kind, and if it requires intelligence to divert disaster, then disaster is absolutely certain. This is a condition which, more than anything else, attracts the attention of the student and creates deep apprehension on the part of all who wish to save modern civilization.
As my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) very ably pointed out, this situation is universal; it is not merely Canada which we are discussing when we talk about unemployment. Just for a moment I should like to refer very briefly to some figures. The London Daily Herald, which may be regarded as the mouthpiece of organized labour in Great Britain, estimates that to-day there are 30,000,000 unemployed in the civilized world,

Unemployment-Mr. Irvine
and that the crisis extends over the entire globe. There are about 6,000,000 unemployed in the United States; about 4,583,000 idle workers in Germany; approximately 1,000,000 unemployed in Japan, and several millions in Russia. So it goes on. As I say, it is a universal situation, and I do not see any reason why the Prime Minister should have become so angered and displeased to-day because in Canada we arc facing a problem which every government in civilization must face and is facing with at least some degree of sincerity and intelligence.
I would go so far as to say that unemployment is inevitable under an economic system which depends upon machine production, profit and distribution through the wage system. Perhaps enough has been said to demonstrate the effects of modern machinery on this question of unemployment, but I will just add one or two little quotations to the point. I should like to read one short extract from an article which appeared in a recent issue of the New Republic:
As a result of labour's growing productivity, American manufacturers were able to get along with over 400,000 fewer men in 1927 than in 1923, and to reduce their wage bill by nearly $160,000,000. In the meantime, the value of factory output increased by over two billions. The consequence was that the wage bill dropped from 18.2 per cent to 17.3 per cent of the gross value of factory product.
One more quotation:
Still more important is the record of profits. ' Between 1923 and 1925, the profits of a group of 403 manufacturers and mining corporations increased 29 per cent. Between 1925 and 1928, the profits of a larger group (574 in all) increased 27 per cent, to a new high record. This makes a gain of nearly 64 per cent between 1923 and 1928. The National City bank reports that the earnings of 375 industrial corporations during the first quarter of 1929 were_ 37 per cent above the corresponding period in 1928. "Many concerns," says the bank in its July review of business, "have in six months made more profits than in the year 1928."
Surely this statement, which is not an isolated one, could be taken as evidence of the effect of machine production on unemployment.
One honourable statesman across the aisle has suggested that the unemployed should go back to the farms. It must be apparent to anyone who is studying this situation that industrialization of agriculture will have the same effect as has the industrialization of other branches of industry. Farmers by the use of machinery are enabled to produce more with half the labour necessary twenty years ago. I quote from Saturday Night, which
should be authoritative to hon. gentlemen opposite, as follows:
During the past 20 years the farm population (of the United States) has decreased nearly 5.500,000. Figures of the bureau of agricultural economics show that the farm population of the United States in 1909 was 32,000,000. In 1929 this had decreased to 27,511,000. About
1.960.000	persons left the farms last year,
1.978.000	in 1927 and 2,155,000 in 1926.
Those who expect to settle the unemployment situation by settling people on the farm will have to face the fact of possible unemployed agriculturists. In fact, these men from the farms are flocking to the cities of Canada in hundreds and thousands, and are aggravating the problem which is already acute.
One of the factors to be considered as a cause of unemployment is the supplanting of men by machinery, the effects of which will be increased as time goes on. Another factor in our economic system which inevitably causes unemployment is known as the profit system. I am not speaking against that system, although I would do so readily if that were pertinent to the discussion.
My intention is to find out the effect of the profit system upon unemployment. Some other time I may extend my argument, but at present I desire only to show that the system under which we are operating, the profit system, makes unemployment inevitable. Why? Because the price of all manufactured goods includes not only all the overhead expense involved in manufacturing, but, as well, a little more than the amount expended, otherwise there can be no profit. Will any hon. gentleman in this house tell me where that "little more" is to come from? Will any hon. gentleman say that there is available as purchasing power among the masses of the people any other money than that which has been distributed in the processes of production? Since in order to realize a profit a manufactured article must be sold for more money than was expended in its production, the result must be that less goods are sold than were actually produced. That is to say, there must inevitably remain a surplus of goods at the end of every producing year. Those goods are placed upon the shelves in our warehouses; next year additional goods are added, and by manufacturers, who of course cannot afford to manufacture goods for pleasure, are forced to discharge their man and again by that act the purchasing power of the country is further reduced. This state of affairs progresses until we reach the very bottom of what we call the period of depression.
The first factor in our system which tends to create unemployment is the supplanting of

Unemployment-Mr. Irvine
human power by mechanical power. The second is the profit system, whereby goods manufactured must be sold for a price greater than the amount of money distributed in their manufacture. Therefore, the total goods manufactured cannot be purchased, which leaves a surplus, and that surplus continually piling up ultimately means unemployment.
Let us look at the third factor, distribution through the wage system. No matter how much we are able to produce, we can distribute only to the extent of the purchasing power of the masses of the people. This is a verj' interesting study, but I do not think I would be thanked by hon. members of the house if I were to consume the remainder of my forty minutes in a discussion of this factor. For the benefit of those hon. gentlemen who may not have thought it worth while to study a question of this kind, I think I should indicate certain works which they could look up for themselves. I would recommend to those hon. gentlemen that they should read what Keynes has to say, and what the Hon. Reginald McKenna has to say. They should read the works of Major Douglas, and those of Maurice Colborne, who gave a performance last week in the city. They should read Arthur Kitson, and Warren Edwin Brokaw. They should read Wells, Shaw, Vowles, Cousins, Wakinshaw and Professor Soddy. Those gentlemen are well able to set forth the principles of what we call the new economics to the full satisfaction of hon. gentlemen who perhaps would not thank me for spending my time in outlining to them those principles.
But perhaps I should expound the point I am dealing with, namely the distribution through the wage system. In the price of an article there is included items which we might designate as A, B, C and D, that is. wages, profits, overhead, replacement of plant, price of raw material, and so forth. Those items of cost must be included in the selling price of an article; therefore, although we may say that the price represents A, B, C and D, the only thing we have with which to buy it is A, and A cannot possibly purchase A plus B, plus C, plus D. There you have the algebra, if you like of this problem.
I would suggest that before a solution can be found for this problem, there must be developed a new aim for industry itself We have to come to the conclusion that merely to find work will not longer be regarded as an intelligent basis of subsistance. It is surely positively ridiculous for us to say that the man who does not work cannot live, when there is not any wrork for the man to do. Why not hang him at once and be done with
[Mr. Irvine.l
it? Why let him have three weeks of misery and hell of mind and body on account of his family when we could get rid of him in an electric chair? Why not be sensible about the matter if that is the only cure hon. gentlemen have for unemployment? If hon. gentlemen are Christian, the electric chair is more Christian than unemployment; it would certainly be much more humane to do that than to do nothing.
Mr. YOUNG CWevburn): Does a doctor kill the man that he cannot cure?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I wish we had some doctor for my hon. friend. I am quite certain he could not cure him and I would not say a word if he did the other thing. In regard to the curse which fell upon mankind, the curse of work, according to the Book which my hon. friend over there follows, the situation has been reversed and now everybody wants to be cursed, everybody wants work. To-day the man who is really cursed is the man who cannot get work. If I had time I should like to tell hon. members I do not want work and I do not want anybody else to work, but until we find a better way of distributing what machinery can produce, I suppose we shall have to stay with the outworn system. If, however, we are going to stay with it we must organize our industrial pursuits and regulate hours of labour so that every man will have an eaual opportunity. We must also stabilize wages on a living basis and not pay men for two hours instead of eight hours when there is not eight hours' work for everybody. That is such an elementary proposh tion, one would expect even a consumers' league to understand it. and yet they do not. It is surely uneconomic to produce goods which are not consumed. Such a condition is of course the defeat of economics, and yet that is what we are doing in Canada and in every other country, namely, producing goods which cannot be consumed because we have not discovered how to get them to the consumers.
I think it is true that the greater the surplus of production, the greater will be the unemployment. In that respect I believe the Prime Minister will have to accept responsibility for unemployment, for he has proved, or tried to prove to us, that last year was the greatest year in production that Canada had ever seen:	it was unprecedented. I
forget all the adjectives which the Prime Minister called to his assistance to express this tremendous output which characterized the industrial life of Canada last year. If he would just study the problem he would find

Unemployment-Mr. Irvine
that this is the very reason why unemployment is greater than it ever was before, because production being so great and there being no market for it, the men are thrown out of employment. The shelves are all filled up with goods, but there is nobody to buy them and nothing to buy them with. So the Prime Minister is probably right when he says that last year we produced more than we did in any previous year and so we have more unemployment now than we had at any other time.
The government is surely not going to try to escape entirely from its responsibility in these matters. To begin with, the government is certainly responsible for the administration of finance. It is responsible, as one hon. gentleman in debate to-night pointed out, for the management of our railway system. It is responsible for the expenditure of money, hundreds of millions of dollars of public money on all kinds of undertakings. It is, or at least it has been up to the present time, responsible for the immigration policy of this country. All these things have a direct bearing upon unemployment, and surely the government is not going to sit here and authorize the bringing in of thousands of immigrants to swell the already over-swollen volume of unemployment, to administer finance without regard to its economic significance, and to get away from the direct responsibility which any self-respecting government ought to be anxious to assume. Refusal by word of mouth to accept responsibility will not be sufficient to enable my hon. friends to escape from it, because responsibility has a way of sticking closer than a brother. The government, as I say, is trying to deny its share of the responsibility. We ought to follow for a moment the idea about greater production and its corollary of unemployment. I notice that the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) and the Prime Minister were both deeply concerned about the farmer in this proposition; indeed, they were solicitous for him. The Prime Minister went even so far as to ask: When did a deputation of agriculturists come to the government and ask for assistance to the unemployed? Since when, for instance, has the Prime Minister been interested in deputations of agriculturists? Did they ever come to him and ask him to increase tariffs against them? I do not think they did, but he did not hesitate to increase them, and he did not hesitate to fail to reduce them. So I am rather surprised that he, having disregarded the farmers before, should now take such an interest in them.
But let me point out that this question of purchasing power which underlies unemployment is the real problem of agriculture as well as of labour. Do hon. members realize that while we had a comparatively small crop last year, nevertheless we could not sell it to advantage nor have we been able to do so as yet, and while we were in the position that we could not get rid of our wheat, millions of people in China were actually starving, unable to get our wheat? There you have internationally the same problem that we have nationally in respect to unemployment. It is a question of money. Moreover we shall have to get the idea that industry is a human proposition. That is, every industry shall be measured, not by its output, not by the size of the payroll, but in terms of the human element which it has turned out. Has our producing system actually produced greater, nobler, wiser and happier men and women? That is the measuring standard I would expect the Prime Minister who wrote Industry and Humanity to use, when considering the problem which we are now discussing. We must have a new function for finance also. It would be interesting, if I had time, to deal with who creates the money, especially when we realize how important the creation of money is to the distribution of goods.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Tell us privately.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will tell my hon. friend
publicly. He will agree with me that there is much more money in circulation in Canada to-day than there was fifty years ago. Where did it come from? Who is the manufacturer of money? Do hon. gentlemen think it snows money? If any hon. gentleman or any gentleman anywhere is entrusted with making money, how do we know he has made enough or too much of it? In any case, who has charge of the matter? Let me give a quotation from Major C. H. Douglas who, in an address on "Where money comes from" before the International Engineering Congress at Tokyo, said:
It is astonishing, when we consider the importance to every one of us of money in our daily life, that most people have no conception of where money comes from beyond a hazy idea that a certain amount of it is dug out of the ground in the form of gold, silver and copper, and the rest of it is printed and issued through a government department. But as a matter of fact money in this form only bears a very trivial relation to the amount of available purchasing power, insufficient as the latter has been stated to be. The total amount of money in circulation, in the form of gold, silver, copper and paper coinage is, in Great Britain, only

Unemployment-Mr. Irvine
about .7 of one per cent of the total amount of bank clearings, or less than 10 per cent of bank deposits, available to be drawn or for purchasing purposes. Money is created by banks in the form of bank credits.
Perhaps we would go a long way towards solving the unemployment problem if we studied the question; who issues the purchasing power which is available to the people of Canada with which to buy goods? There are numerous other quotations that I should like to give, but my time is flying.
There is another statement that I wish to make, and that is that credit control is a very important factor in the prevention of unemployment, or at least in the problem that lies behind unemployment.
Someone has mentioned Fi-ance in this debate. I would mention France first, of course, for the reason that it has no unemployment. But there are two reasons at least why France has no unemployment. First of all, France has had a stationary population for a great many years. The second reason is that France did not deflate and go back to the gold basis after the war. Hon. gentlemen here who were so anxious to rush back to the gold basis, not knowing what they were doing, are now reaping some of the fruits of their stupidity. Some hon. gentleman says that we are not on a gold basis now. That does not worry me. We ought to be forced back to it so that hon. gentlemen would realize fully the result of such a policy. France did not do that, and to-day, according to this morning's Ottawa Citizen, the French franc is worth 4 cents where it used to be worth 20 cents in international exchange, and the Belgian franc is worth still less. But the French and Belgian people have been kept employed. Purchasing power has been maintained at least sufficiently to keep the wheels of industry running steadily. So hon. gentlemen who quote France as having no unemployment had better examine all the factors before rushing to conclusions that such is due to her tariff policy.
Poverty, which results from unemployment, is preventable. Unemployment is the secondary cause of poverty. Poverty itself is preventable. We have the equipment, we have the resources, we have the intelligence, and we have the skill. There used to be a time when it was said that tuberculosis was not preventable, but the doctors got busy and now it is preventable. To-day it is said that cancer is incurable, but the doctors are now working on that. They do not deny their responsibility. Some day they will be successful in finding a cure. Unemployment, I say, is the chief

secondary cause of poverty. Our government denies its responsibility and refuses even to work on the proposition. I want to ask that the government reconsider the position that has been taken by the Prime Minister, and give relief in this unemployment situation, if it is necessary. I do not know whether it is necessary now or not, but we ought to find out. Let the government give a lead and go as far as it can constitutionally to organize a system of unemployment insurance. If after that the provinces do not follow in the manner presented by the constitution we will know where the blame is to be placed. Let a permanent commission be appointed to study this problem until a solution is found.
I want to say something about the Prime Minister's speech. He was very definite about what he cannot do and what he will not do, but very hazy about what we think he ought to do. I think he is obligated to making a an attempt to solve the problem, and we are not going to be satisfied with his old constitutional argument. He says that he does not want to take the taxpayers' money to be expended perhaps in some isolated community in the west or in the east as the case might be. Let me read the admirable words of the right hon. gentleman when he was speaking in this house in 1926, when the old age pension legislation went through. Someone took the objection that such legislation was ultra vires of this parliament, and the Prime Minister said:
In that regard may I say that as between the different provinces I fail to see where there is any distinction to be drawn between the money voted by this parliament, say for the purposes of immigration, which may go to place a man or woman in any one of the provinces, and money voted for preserving the individual, no matter in what part of the Dominion he may be found. Human beings are the greatest of the resources of the country. What we are here considering is human life. An individual, no matter which province he is in, is an asset to the Dominion as a whole, and it is from that point of view that the Dominion is, I think, considering this matter.
If an old gentleman of seventy years of age is an asset to Canada, surely a young man of seventeen or twenty or twenty-seven is an even greater asset; and the very same logic which the Prime Minister applies to old age pensions must be applied to the suggestion put forward by my hon. friend from North Winnipeg. The Prime Minister says that he has had no requests from the provinces for assistance. For obvious reasons. In the first place, they know that it would be useless. In the second place, the provincial premiers do not wish to put themselves into the position of advising the Prime Minister as to his duty and responsibility in regard to this matter,

Unemployment-Mr. MacDonald (C. Breton)
so naturally they may have been a little reticent in this regard.
I am sorry that the Prime Minister felt called upon to state that he would not give five cents of the money from the public treasury of this Dominion to a Tory provincial government anywhere. I will not say much about that because I feel sure that the Prime Minister was not quite himself when he said it. I mean to say that he is usually so courteous and generous in debate, but today he was angry and said things that I feel sure he himself will be sorry for. I do not think that that is the practice of the Prime Minister. I think he is bigger than that.
The Prime Minister went on to place the blame on the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada for his having failed to call an economic conference. If that is true the congress will have to answer to organized labour.
I shall conclude my references to the Prime Minister's speech by recalling his remarks in connection with the argument of my hon. friend from Bow River. The Prime Minister indicated in his closing remarks that the attitude of the hon. member for Bow River was that everything that could be known about this subject was known already, and therefore there was no need to appoint any commission to investigate. I think that the shafts of the right hon.. gentleman's sarcarsm went very wide the mark. If he will examine the speech of the hon. member for Bow River, he will find that the hon. member was merely asking for an economic commission to find a solution for the problem. That is where I think the Prime Minister missed the point.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The subject brought up by the
amendment of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) is one in which I am deeply interested. I have the honour to represent a county that is entirely industrial, being comprised largely of coal miners and steel workers. We have no leisured class in my county, and every man and woman in it is intensely interested in the question of unemployment. The amendment itself asks the house to declare that the government should take immediate action to deal with the question of unemployment. It is probably in its terms a little narrow, but in the course of the discussion that has taken place this afternoon a very wide range of subjects has been covered. Possibly the amendment is so worded as to admit discussion not only on the question of unemployment but also on the causes and the cure, if a cure can be found. The discussion, as I have said, has taken a wide
range. For the most part it has consisted of theories; we have heard various theories discussed by hon. members, ranging over distribution, consumption, finance, industry, capital-anything having the nearest or remotest relation to unemployment has been discussed. But, as was pointed out by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), in his quotation of a remark by Grover Cleveland, it is a condition and not a theory that confronts us. An ordinary person, if he were asked what is the cure for unemployment, would naturally say "work." It is far better to give a man work than to give him insurance against unemployment. And it is to that feature of the question that I intend to address most of my remarks.
We on this side of the house contend, rightly or wrongly, that the fiscal policy of the government is largely responsible for the unemployment in this country at the present time, and I propose to submit some facts in support of my contention. I listened to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) yesterday, and I may tell him frankly that I sympathize with him. I understand how difficult is his position. I know he felt that he had not been successful in getting his colleagues in the cabinet to see eye to eye with him in labour matters. I fully appreciate the difficulty he had in trying to defend the action of the government in regard to labour conditions. Not only do I sympathize with him, I appreciate the importance of his position, as I know he does. He speaks articulately for labour in this country, and in my opinion there is no portfolio more important, more fraught with good or evil towards a great body of our people than the portfolio he holds. I listened to his speech and I congratulate him on one aspect of it-it was probably as good a defence of his position and the position of the government as could be made; and although the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to-day employed the same arguments that the Minister of Labour used yesterday, in my opinion he made no better defence.
I understood the Minister of Labour to rest his defence on three grounds. First-and in this possibly the Prime Minister went further than did the Minister of Labour; he said there was really no unemployment problem in this country at the present time. The Minister of Labour did not go that far; as a matter of fact he said he was not stating that there was no question of unemployment confronting us; he admitted there was. As I say, the Prime Minister went a little further. On the strength of not having received any word
1266	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. MacDonald (C. Breton)
from the premiers of the various provinces, he boldly stated that unemployment did not prevail to any serious extent. In short, the Prime Minister made an election speech; but, [ repeat, I do not think he made as good a defence of his government as did the Minister of Labour.
The second ground taken by the Minister of Labour was that unemployment was just as bad in other countries. He may be right. But he spent most of his time in dealing with totally irrelevant matters-the construction of the trans-Canada highway and questions of local interest that have absolutely nothing to do with unemployment. The impression we all received from the speeches of the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister is that the government is opposed to the idea of unemployment insurance. There is no question that the government is so opposed.
The third ground was that the Minister of Labour had ordered a great deal of work to be done, and had gone out of his way to ask the railways to provide employment. But unfortunately he did not go into particulars in that respect and show us how much work he had ordered and how much employment he had persuaded the railways to provide. I think the Minister of Labour made a mistake in trying to place responsibility on the Conservative party for something they had done in order to justify the stand he was taking. He quoted, in part, from an order in council for the purpose of showing that the Conservatives in days gone by had said that unemployment was a municipal question. But when he had to read the whole order in council, it threw a very different light on the question, and I think the minister would have been far better advised had he confined himself to a straight story of what he had done and what he proposed to do to meet the unemployment situation. Also, he was a little indefinite in defending the speech he made at London. That was a forward-looking speech for him to make. We all recognize that when a minister makes a public statement he binds his government, that is, if the government is guided by the usual constitutional principle of cabinet solidarity. We find now that the interpretation placed on his London speech was not justified by any action the government had taken or proposed to take. The Minister of Labour has put himself in a false position with regard to the labour of this country:	he makes a stetement on a
public platform as to what he intends to do and what the Prime Minister and the government will back him up in doing, and when he comes to the House of Commons and is ques-
tioned about it, the Prime Minister absolutely refuses to back him up, and takes a different ground altogether. With regard to unemployment, in my view there is only one cure, and that is work. Has this government been guilty of any act, either legislative or administrative, that has injured employment in Canada? After all, employment insurance is a good thing only under certain circumstances. We in Cape Breton would hold up both hands for it if we could get it. Every winter we are faced with this problem. During the summer months we ship our coal by water, but in the winter months, when water transportation is not available, the mines have to work on half or quarter time, and the men through no fault of their own have to be idle. They are willing and anxious to work, and would be quite content to enter into any scheme of contributory unemployment insurance.
The idea behind insurance is one of security. There are three things, of course, that the labouring man wants: first, fair wages; second, fair hours; third, security in his work. For the present we may dispense with consideration of the first two. It is the principle of security for the man disabled at work which underlies unemployment insurance. That principle was recommended to this government in the Mathers report away back in 1921. I am going to read from sections 35 and 36:
35.	This is something which affects all wage earners, but more especially the casual labourer. He can never be sure just when his employment will terminate and he will be left without the means of subsistence.
36.	Unemployment may arise from other causes than the loss of his job. He may be incapacitated by sickness, invalidity or old age. Very few labourers are able, out of their earnings, to make provision for these contingencies. We recommend to your government the question of making some provision by a system of state social insurance for those who through no fault of their own are unable to work, whether the inability arises from lack of opportunity, sickness, invalidity or old age. Such insurance would remove the spectre of fear which now haunts the wage earner and make him a more contented and better citizen.
In what way does the fiscal policy of this government affect the question of unemployment? Take, for instance, the item of coal. The coal mines are idle for perhaps five months of the year. We import in the vicinity of 13,000,000 tons of coal from the United States, and last year we sent them $54,000,000 of our money. We have ample coal in this country in the eastern and western sections to meet all domestic demands for that commodity. For three or four years those of us who come from coal-producing counties have

Unemployment-Mr. MacDonald (C. Breton)
been urging upon the government the desirability of inaugurating a national fuel policy. Instead of that, however, we find imports of coal from other countries increasing every year, and this year we have the additional news that 250,000 tons of coal from Soviet Russia will be brought into Canada. That is a serious matter for us, because such an importation will displace a certain amount of our coal. Three years ago I submitted to this government in my remarks on the budget a proposition by which a national fuel policy could be evolved. Instead of that the government contented itself with bringing down the bonus to coking plants bill. There never was, I suppose, in the history of all the legislation brought into this house a bigger piece of fake legislation than that coke ovens bill. It pretended to offer a subsidy for the creation of coke ovens in Canada. Three years have gone by and needless to say not a dollar has been granted under the bill, because nobody has applied for it. Nobody ever will apply for it so long as the policy of this country is to allow coke into Canada free of duty, and to give a rebate on coal brought in for the purpose of producing coke. We can supply all the coal that is needed; all we want is a sensible suggestion as to how we can solve this problem, because it is not beyond the power of man to do it. Two or three days ago I got a letter from my home town stating that 500 men had been laid off the steel works there because there was no work for them. Yet every day one million dollars' worth of iron and steel products is brought into this country. This government, since it came into power, has lowered the duty on fifty-five different items in the iron and steel schedule.
Is there any connection between the fiscal policy of the present government and unemployment in Canada to-day? Theories may be all right, but the moment you subject them to the acid test of practical business principles they go to the wind. While the Utopian theories and ideas of world revolution are all very fine and may come to pass centuries hence, the question for us at the present time is to deal with the immediate problems that face us. My submission is that until there is a different outlook on the part of the government things will be very little better so far as unemployment is concerned. I think it was the hon. member for Bow River who said he did not think the result was so very different whether we had protection or free trade. I may be a bit of a free trader myself, up to a certain limit; I believe in free trade in boots and shoes, hats and caps, clothing, furniture and flour, but I am not a
free trader with regard to coal and steel. When it comes to coal and steel I want a duty, but I cannot get that duty unless I give the other fellow protection on hats, caps, boots, shoes, clothing and furniture, and I am willing to do that because I am satisfied that it is the only way I can get what I consider to be necessary.
Let me say just a word or two in regard to the constitutional question. If ever a smoke screen was thrown around a subject, it has been the case with regard to the invoking of the British North America Act in connection with this matter, and the statement that primarily it is one for the provinces or the municipalities to deal with. I say it is nothing of the kind. In 1864, when the British North America Act was being framed, the statesmen of that day who builded better than they knew could not foresee everything that was likely to happen. They did hand over something to the provinces and the provinces in turn handed it over to the municipalities, where we now have what is known as the Poor Relief Act. Under that act, which I assume is practically the same in nearly all the English speaking provinces, a man who has a settlement in a particular district and who is in need of support is entitled to get it from that district. If he has no settlement there but has a settlement in some other part of the province of Nova Scotia, he can be moved there where he will receive his support. If he has his settlement outside the province then the province has to take the responsibility of sending him to that outside district where he belongs. Beyond that the Dominion government must step in and deport the man if necessary, so the so-called constitutional aspect of this question is not a factor at all.
The question of unemployment is one which affects all the people of Canada, and we cannot take it away from this government by handing it over to the municipalities. I think the Minister of Labour made that clear in his speech at London. He stated that his idea was that a system should be inaugurated which would be suitable to Canadian needs. He said:
Take, for example, our Canadian railroad workers-in the summer time there are upwards of 200,000 men employed, and during the winter periods there are about 25,000 of those workers laid off for several months. The wages of all railwaymen average about $130 per month. If a fund were created, it would take about $5,000,000 to pay these employees half-pay for three months.
The Minister of Labour knows very well that no province could undertake anything of that sort; any such system must come from

this government. In the light of these facts and with the knowledge possessed by the minister, why should he try to throw the responsibility on the provinces?
Another question which is very pertinent is this:	The Prime Minister himself said
the provinces had not asked for such a scheme and that no demand had been made for it.

Yes, I know that; this suggested solution of the problem might be all right, but it never can be carried out by one province with regard to a railway system which passes through seven or eight provinces. Not one of these provinces could bring such a scheme into operation, because of the fact that the railway crosses so many other provinces as well. The very illustration given by the minister shows how futile is his suggestion that it is a matter for the provinces.
The Prime Minister also says that the provinces never have asked for this scheme. The provinces did not ask for the old age pensions scheme; why was it forced upon them. That legislation was passed in this house without the provinces having been consulted; general legislation was passed and the provinces were invited to take part in it. The same thing could be done here; it might be worked out on the same basis as workmen's compensation. There is no difficulty and no obstacle in the way of putting this unemployment insurance in force if only you are honest about it. Unemployment insurance should be on an actuarial basis, as is the case with all other forms of insurance.
